And Pain Saddened her Youth.

• "A sad change came over my daughter in her teens.' She became languid - and melancholy, and the roses left her cheeks; her lips and gums were quite bloodless, and it was pitiable to see her. suffer. "So nervous was she that any noise would make, her tremble; also, she dreaded being alone. Her strength vanished, and she often fainted. "A specialist said she was suffering from Anwmia, Neuralgia and Heart Weakness, but in spite of clever treat- ment she remained in the same weak, bloodless state. "At length I gave her a course of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and after a time I noticed a pleasing difference in her health. She improved in appearance and her nerves were strengthened; she was always bright and well, and the pains _round her heart and fainting fits ceased. Her cheeks glowed with a good colour, and her appetite was quite restored. Since her cure she,,has remained strong and full of energy.

div.head: Dr. Williams' Pink Pills
div.p: Dr. Williams' Pink Pills
The Chitin Nitrate Fields.

In view of the fact that even now there exis'e an erroneous impression as to the length of life of these deposits, the recent report of the Chilian Govern- ment's Inspector of Nitrate Propaganda, Senor Alejandro Bertrand, on this subject is interesting and instructive. Unfortunately our space will not permit our giving it in full, but the following extract is suffi- cient to show that there is no fear of the beds being exhausted for many years to come. In his report the Inspector says I could from the first have contradicted the rumours to the effect that the beds in question would he exhausted in the near future,for in 1892,when I held the office of fiscal delegate at Iquique, I made an estimate of the land which had been explored and sampled up-to-date, arriving at n minimurn'total of 110 million tons. Of this 140 million tons, 20 million have been exported during the period of 15 years which have since elapsed, so that there still remained at least 120 million tons in the beds explored up to that period. While as a matter of fact during these 15 years, not only have numerous fresh beds been discovered, but it has been ascertained that the extent of those previously known is much larger than that set forth in the above-mentioned estimate. My Govern ment, in response to my urgent request, for official figures, has just sent me a specially drawn up report furnished by their delegate in the nitrate district, on the extent of the beds which have not yet been worked. These are accessible by rail, have been thoroughly explored, and for the most part their extent estimated; it is therefore an easy matter to approximately deter- mine the nitrate they will yield, thus arriving at a minimum stock on which commerce will undoubtedly to be able to rely. By adding to this stock the figures resulting from the explorations and operations of boring, which are being continually carried out, and deducting the figures exported in proportion, we shall be able to prepare every year an inventory of the minimum quantity of nitrate on which we can rely in the future. The surface of the fields containing nitrate in the hands of private companies in the Province of Tarapaca cover an area of .39 square kilometres each of which is estimated to yield an Overage of 90,000 tons. If, however, we reduce the estimate by ono-third, thus bringing it to 60-000 tons, the contents of these fields would still be in round numbers 28 million tons of nitrate. The lots of Neal grounds measured, bored and esti- ted in the Province of Tamp:lea cover an acre of 59 kilometres, containing 6 million tons of nitrate, or snore than 100,000 tons per kilometre, which proves our figure of 60,000 tons per kilometre for the private grounds to be very moderate. In the Province of Antofagasta, 3,780 square kilo- metres of land have been measured, but our information respecting their contents up to the present time only extends to about 1,000 square kilometres, and would warrant our taking a minimutn of 61,000 tons per kilo- metre. We, however, reduce these figures to 50,0 0 tons, which leave us in round numbers, a total quantity of 186 million tons of nitrate for the fleld3 of Antofagasta Thus we get these figures : Province or Tarapaca—private owners... 28 million tons D.). 1130,1 land Province of Antoragasto... 186

220 , We can therefore assure the nitrate industi'y of a MINIMUM STOCK OF' 220 MILLION TONS. No allowance whateyer is made for the unexplored lands in the nitrate region, so that the farmer may rest assured that there is no fear of the supply failing for a Century at least."

Dr. Newton H. Marshall in the introduction to a work on which he has been engaged for many tnonths says " The dearth'of theological writings dealing with the distinctively Christian life in any of its aspects is remarkable enough. The absence of works of any scientific value dealing with Conversion and Holiness is still more notable." He explains that of the twelve hundred volumes mentioned in the "Theological Encyclopaedia" there is only one dealing directly with Conversion. There should therefore be plenty of room for Dr. Marshall's new book "Conversion of the New Birth " which is announced to be issued early in March by the National Free Church Council. This is the third volume in the "Christian Faith and Doctrine" series edited by the Rev. F. B. Meyer, B.A. •

What of Miss Dorothy Drew.—Among the debntantes to be presented at the forthcoming Courts, w ill be Miss Dorothy Drew, the favourite grandchild, and constant companion at home of Mr. W. E. Gladstone, in his ; later years. She will probably be presented by her aunt, Mrs. Herbert Gladstone, but Miss Drew, who is a tall, fair, slender girl of twenty, has been staying with her mother at Dublin Castle, and made her formal entrance into Society at the recent Vicersal entertain- ments. Miss Drew is a clever girl who has read a great deal, and her appearance not long since on Mr. Churchill's platform at Manchester indicates that she inherits the family traditions in politics. Forthcoming Weddings.—The marriage of Lord Douro and Miss Maud Coats, whose engagement was recently announced,is to take place next month, and will be one of the fashionable early spring weddings. Lord Douro is the eldest of the four sons of the Duke and Duchess of Wellington, and Mies Maud Coats is the younger daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George Coats, who are extremely wealthy, and well-known in social circles in London. The announcement of the forthcoming marriage of Lord Dalmeny and Miss Dorothy Grosvenor is also of interest., and the wedding will be a notable event in fashionable society. Lord Delmeny is the elder son of the Earl of Rosebery, and nearly related to the Rothschild family, whilst Miss Dorothy Grosvenor is a daughter of the widowed Lord Henry Grosvenor, and corigin of the Duke of Westminster. , The death of the Duke of Westminster's son will place the numerous members of the Grosvenor family in ! mourning, and it will therefore be a quiet wedding. Beauty Patches.—Hitherto we have been accustomed to see beauty patches worn only on the stage, or at fancy dress balls, hut a few of fashion's votaries have been seen wearing the little black spots or half-moons on their faces on ordinary occasions. The wearing of these patches was intended in the old days to make the eyes look brighter and larger, and the eyes smaller, but a very perfect pink and white complexion is needed to wear them to advantage. To a muddy or spotty com- plexion they only make the defects more conspicuous, hence came the powdering and elaborate" make-up "of the woman of fashion in Queen Anne's reign. To modern tastes, the black patch would appear nuite unnatural and inartistic, and it is not at all likely that this old-time fashionable will be taken up again by the outside world of women. Vulgar Lavishness.—Cotillon favours have grown more and more costly during the past two or three years, and nowadays rich folk, wealthly Americans especially, think little when giving a ball, of spending over a thousand pounds upon such presents. Diamond rings, tie pins, studs, and earrings ; long gem-set chains, and braclets ; lace fans, opera glasses, etc., find a place on the list, and at one or two of the balls given lately, the scramble to obtain more than a right share of these good things was worthy rather of the traditions ef Whitechapel than of Mayfair—and in one particular instance, nearly resulted in a scandal. Black to the Fore Again.—Black net gowns, much. embroidered with jet, and worn over soft black satin underdresses, are in high favour. Generally speaking, jet may be said to look its best alone, yet it is not infrequently united with steel and silver, and some women even prefer the net overdress mounted upon white or pale-coloured satin. The all-black notion however, with the jet reigning in single blesseclness,and a jet ornament either in a coronet, wreath, or aigrette form, arranged in the hair, is decidedly smarted. Irish Poplin.—Ottoman silk is having a considerable vogue for tailor-mades, but as the summer advances, it will almost certainly give way to Shantung. For Spring however, ottoman silk is exceedingly modish wear, especially in the new, and vary beautiful steel- blue tones, and trimmed with cut-stNal buttons. At the moment there are rumours to the effect that Irish poplin will be greatly in evidencen little later on, which is good bearing to those who would fain see the home industries prospering, and who would secure, at com- paratively low prices, a fabric that always looks well, and practically never wears out. More About Sleeves.—Sleeves to the amateur dress- maker are worrying items just now. The perfectly plain, and tightly-fitting specimen—which by the way is becoming to very few, is difficult to fashion and set into the armhole. It is apt to drag in some parts and bag in others, as many of us are painfully aware. One way out of the trouble is to add a little over-sleeve, reaching half-way to the elbow, and slashed up the opening being loosely laced across with ribbons, or bands of the fabric, such trimming appearing upon the yoke. Another idea is to arrange a little puff at the op of the sleeve, which affords the generally desirable width and relieves the monotony of the long line., Perhaps the most becoming sleeve that for many years past has fallen to our lot, is one we have lately parted with namely, the long loop to the elbow, and from them tightly fitting to the wrist. The Smell of Paint.—Soon the annual " earthquake " will be under consideration, at any rate in those apart- ments in which firts are a forbidden luxury. No doubt it is well to begin early, especially wh(n new paint is the order of the day, always provided of course the household generally can tolerate a brisk and perchance icy breeze, and are not afraid of copious draughts. A capital plan during the painting process, which by the way causes many people considerable distress, is to place large shallow boats of water about the room. If the expense does not matter, milk should be substituted for water. The milk will be found to re3uce the smell of paint in a room, in a most remarkable degree,

Cheaper Food.—Food generally, according to market reports, is cheaper than it was, hut the, housewife seldom seems to get the benefit of a fall in prices. Farmers, it is said, are getting Bs. to 10s. per head less for their sheep than they were a year no. yet the butchers charges remain much the same. Like the coal merchants, and the provision dealers, they are ready enough to put up their prices when excuse offers, but are slow to reduce them in times of abnormal cheapness. The Contract Committee of the Metropolitan Asylum Board, may be accepted as a fairly reliable authority on ruling prices, and judging by this report the public should be having the benefit of cbeapr meat, bread, cheesemongery, and some groceries.

div.head: DANCING BY DAYLIGHT.
div.p: DANCING BY DAYLIGHT.

Someone told •me the other day, writes " Algernon " in the Gentlewoman, that after- noon, dances are being introduced into some country districts, and have obtained a certain vogue. I cannot believe that this form of .en- tertainment will really become popular. Dancing by daylight gives one the same sort ot dissipated feeling as .playing bridge in a gar(l:?,n on a fine summer's afternoon. Then there is also the question of costume—it would be exceedingly difficult to decide what exactly would be the correct " wear " for an •afternoon dance. Even more serious, I should think, would be the question of get- ting partners for the young ladies. Dancing men tare difficult enough to procure, even when they can look- in at their own time in the evening, and have the prospect of a first- • rate supper after midnight. Even if business did not interfere, one can hardly imagine the jeunesse doree taking • the floor in the middle of the afternoon, with the prospect of tea and ;laret cup only to fortify the inner-man.

div.head: NEW SKIRT.
div.p: A NEW SKIRT.

Pictured in our illustration is a skirt of the very latest and mot - up-tn-date type. This. model comes from a famous Paris house, and is the very latest word on the subject of skirts. It is realised in fine smooth cloth of medium weight and of a charming, tone of mole colour. The upper part is of the correct

modified corselet shape, just high enough to do away with any necessity for a waistband. The skirt itself is formed of two close-fitting tunics placed one over the other in novel and most, attractive stYle. Below the lower tunic the skirt falls in soft folds to the feet. It is very long all round, and quite decidedly trained at the back. The tunics, I should not omit to say, come to a deep point in the middle of the back.

div.head: Too MUCII LIBERTY.
div.p: Too MUCII LIBERTY.

Public taste at the moment is deplorable, but that is scarcely a. reason, declares "Lady Phyllis " in the World, •why the newspapers of England, instead of endeavcuring to raise, should pander to it. Nothing is sacred now, nothing is, apparently—well, quite, the re- verse of sacred! . The most detestable details of divorce cases are printed in respectable ( !) journals; notoriety, while it is sought by the modern, is welcomed; mere adventurers and adventuresses are lauded to the skies, feted, financed, and proposed to, till half the silly, weak-brained persons feel it shabby and almcst wrong to earn a decent, ordinary, re- spectable living. - Murders and suicides are the topics of the hour, trogedies reign supreme, people who are tco cowardly to stop and face life in this world leave letters that saints might have written—only these latter would never hove been so cheeky; and such thing are published till pity, yes, and sym- pathy, lies with the wrongdoer. Virtue is going out of fashion; vice, so it be sufficiently melodramatic, is sure of a hearing. -

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

CANNELONS OF VEAL.—Six tablespoonfuls of chopped lean cold veal, two teaspoonfuls of chopped cooked ham, six chopped pre- served mushrooms, the yolks of two eggs, a small teacupful of white sauce, three-quarters of a pound of puff pastry. Flour some round Wooden sticks about four inches Jong; the handles of old wooden spoons would do. Roil the pastry out to the thickness of an eighth of an inch. Cut it into long strips about an inch wide, • Twist these loosely round the sticks, letting the 'edge S overlap each other in the twists. Bake them in a hot oven until they are a pale brown. Allow the pastry to cool a little, then gently draw out the sticks. Mix the veal, ham, and mushrooms, put them into a saucepan with the sauce and stir over the fire until the mixture is hot, add the yolks of the eggs, and stir for a minute longer. Season. carefully, then fill in the cannelons with the mixture. Leave them until cold, and serve mem garnished with parsley or watercress. If a hot dish is preferred, heat the cannelons slowly in the oven. - The remains of any kind af cold meat may be used in the place of val.

div.head: MARRIED LADY TEACHERS.
div.p: MARRIED LADY TEACHERS.
DRASTIC PROPOSAL DISCUSSED BY THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

A proposal of considerable interest and importance with reference to the employment of married women as teachers in the schools of.lVarrington, nas discussed at the meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday evening. It was introduced by Mr. T. P. Bradshaw and took the following form : "That the managers of public elementary schools end the School Management Committee be instructed to give three months' notice in writing to terminate, on the last day of June, 1909, the engagements of all married female teachers at presunt on their staffs, and that after that date, this authority will not recognise _ _ _

nor pay tha salary of any married female teacher. Before the resolution was proposed, Mr. C. S. BURGESS asked the chairman to rule the resolution out of order on the ground that it was ultra vircs. lie maintained that it was beyond the power of the com- mittee to instruct the managers of non-provided schools to.discuss teachers, whether male or female, upon any but educational grounds. Mr. 11. ROBERTS : This is an educational ground. _ _

Mr. BURGESS quoted the terms of the Clause on which he relied and raid he bad given notice of his question in order that the Law Clerk to the authority might he consulted about it. The CHAIRMAN (Councillor Fulton Smith) said he had consulted the Town Clerk who told him the resolu- tion was quite in order on the educational point. Mr. Bradshaw said be was advised by the Director of Education some time ago that the resolution was in strict accordance with the ruling of the Board of Education. He hoped tha committee would consider the question from a businesslike and commonsense standpoint and not from the sentimental point of view. There was no gainsaylng the fact that there had been a vigorous canvass by certain members of the teaching profession who would be affected by the resolution, with a view to its being defeated. They would prob- ably le told that the School Management Committee had already passed a resolution to the effect that they did not intend to employ any more married women teachers in the Borough, but he thought that was an admission that the principle of employing such teachers was wrong. It might be contended that in 1903 there was a half-hearted arrangement between the married teachers and the School Management Committee that tbose who were then employed should not be disturbed, but even if that were so,surely an arrangement passed in 1903 was not going to bind the committee in existence in 1909. Further, he had mcde inquiries at the Educa- tion Office and could not find record of any such arrangement having been made. It would be admitted on all hands that there were hundreds of certificatedl teachers throughout the country who were unable to obtain employment, and who would not be able to gain it until the committees discharged the hundreds of married women who were taking their places. The resolution if ctrried would affect ten teachers in War- rington, and seeing that they bad sixteen pupil teachers who wee leaving college and would he acceptable for appointments in 1909, be would like to ask the Com- mittee where they were going to be employed in this or any other town ? Thero was no doubt that assistant mistresses coming out of college were unable to secure appointments on account of the profession being over- stocked. He telieved there were hundreds of certified teachers who passed through colleges last year and had not jet been able to gain employment. Ile would draw attention to a glaring case which be thought Mr. Burgers was intending to shield by raising his legal objiction, and that was the case of the headmistress of Fairfield schnols. Mrs. Stansfb-ld was engaged at a salary of £l5O a year, from April Ist, 1909, and Mr. Starslield himself was emplo3ed by the authority at a salary of ow a year, with an additional £l6 or £l7 per ar•num for evenineschool work. He maintained that Mr. Stanrfleld and the husbands of the other married teachers were in a financial position sufficient .to maintain their wives,and he was strongly opposed to any certificated teachers being kept out of employment 1 Mr. E. PLINSTON seconded.

• The Bev. Canon STEVENSON said the was thoroughly in agreement with Mr. 13radshaw ns a matter of prin- ciple and one of the first things the School Manage- ment Cofumittee did was to lay down a rule upon which they had consistently acted over since, that they would not appoint any more married women as teachers except in the case of temporary employment. They, however, felt that it would be a hard thing to interfere with the existing appointinents of teachers who had been appointed since 1902. At the present moment there was one lady teacher in this tows who was within a very short time indeed of corapletin her sixty-fifth year. when she would be entitled to a pension. It seemed to him that it would be a cruel thing to dismiss her and rob her of the pension she otherwise would receive. He ventured to hope that Mr.l3radshaw would not press his motion but would be content with what was certainly the fact—that there were only a few married women teachers in the town and in the natural course of things it could not be very long before they would pass away and be no more. As to temporary teachers, that was another matter. It was sometimes extremely difficult to find at a moment's notice, when a teacher was ill, a good teacher to take her place. Some married teenei:. had rendered very valuable services In such emergencies and-it would be a very great pity to cut off that source of stipply.As to the over-stocking of the market, that was, lie regretted to say, perfectly true and no one appreciated it more keenly than he who had large numbers of young students to place. At she same time, not even for that bait would be try to do what to his mind was an injury and an injustice to certain people who had long and faithfully given their services to the education of children in this town. Councillor W. B. ROBERTS opposed the motion, as he thought it would be an iniquitous thing if they refused to acknowledge their moral obligations to those people who had served them for many years. Let them make the resolution prospective, but certainly not retrospective. .

Mr.'UNsworrnr contended that the motion was too wide. It would prevent any woman who separated from her husband through no fault of her own from earning her own livelihood. It was for that reason that scores of gTrls studied and became efficient and got. their certificates to provide against such contingencies. The resolution was not framed with sufficient care. Mr. BURGESS said when be raised the point of order, he had no particular teacher in his mind. He simply thought the committee had no power under the Act to dismiss any teacher on the grounds other than educa- tional—which he took to mean if they were not fitted from an educational point of view to do their work. He protested against what he considered an interfer- ence with the rights of managers of non-provided schools. The Act of Parliament gave the managers the right to appoint and dismiss teachers without any interference on the part of the local education authority. He agreed with the last speaker that the resolution. was loosely worded. He supposed widows were married persons and the resolutions eid not exclude them. Mr. H. ROBERTS: It does, distinctly. Councillor WILKINSON supported the resolution. He complained that inWarrington they had several married lady teachers who were well "under foot." They had sixteen girls coming out of college who were waiting for the ten places now held by married women. Canon Stevensdh said they had no right to interfere with , existing agreements. When the education authority was established in Warrineton they sent the scythe round ruthlessly? and cleared out Article 50 teachers, and told them they must either get certificates or they could not be employed. The position which Canon Stevenson was now taking up with regard to married lady teachers was not consistent with the committee's action in those days. At the time there was a scarcity lof certificated teachers there was some reason for employing married teachers but now, when there was an over-abundance of certificated teachers,there was no place for them. There were large numbers of girls whose parents bad spent money they could ill-afford on their training and now they were sitting by their friends with nothing to do. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH believed that the teachers had paid a certain amount to the Government, so that when they reached a certain age they would get their pension. If this resolution was carried all that money would be wasted and they would be turned adrift. • Mr. UPSON Tbey will get their proportion. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH ' • Who will give it them back? Mr. UPSON : The Government. Mr. FAIRCLOCGII : I have never seen the Govern- ment give anything back yet. (Laughter.) Continuing, be said that irrespective of the pension question it would be a great injustice to teachers who had given faithful service for so limy years to be discharged because someone else wanted their places. Alderman BEN:kn.:TT agreed with Mr. Fairclough and epposed the motion. There might be something to be said for the broad, general principle, and the committee had recognized it by discontinuing the appointment of married Avow n. It would, however, be a distinct, hardship to dismiss people who had served them faith- fully in the past without any idea that this sword of Dornicles was hanging over their heads. The only argument brought .forward in favour of the resolution was that the profession was overcrowded. He had never heard of any- pleasant well-paid profession which was not quickly overcrowded. The teaching profession was without a doubt the Vest paid female profession, and there was a rush into it, and be did not blame girls for wanting to become teachers. here were two obvi, us remedies for overcrowding. One was to increase the vigour of the examinations and admit only the cream of those competing, and the other was to recon- sider the scale. He did not like to be considered mean, but if there was any class proportionately well paid, and perhaps better paid than any other class, it was the teaching profession and particularly the female members of it. He did not see why teachers who bad given faithful service in the past should be treated shabbily. To discharge all the married teachers in Warrington would only be a drop in the bucket, and the overcrowding questiojir could not be appreciably dealt with by any such paltry measures. The Article 50 teachers had been mentioned, but there was no parallel between the two classes. The married teachers were persons pre-eminently qualified by long experience in their profession, and probably they knew more about the teaching profession than anybody else. The one lady

'election Mr. Arthur Peacock, who lived next door to him, came to him and made inquiries about a motor car. What was actually said at that interview did not much matter, but it was plain that Arthur Peacock was willing to give 50s. or £3 to hire a motor car for the election day. As a matter of fact, Mr. Arthur Peacock did hire a motor car, and gave 50s. for it, and came over on the 2nd November from Liscard to Warrington. Mr. Frank Wilkinson saw him start,and it was strongly in favour of Frank Wilkinson's evidence, that while he said that he saw two sons of Arthu: Peacock and the driver, he could not tell who the other person in the car was. He could not identify him. It was admittedly Arthur Peacock, and if Frank IVilkinson had wished to make out a stronger case or in any way to bolster up his evidence, he could easily have said Arthur Peacock was in the motor car. However, he did not and that was enormously in favour of the truth of what he said. It was admitted that Arthur Peacock came over on election day in that car with his two boys and that he said he was giving his two boys a treat. lie never had done such a thing befit-a and the whole of them could have got to iVarrington and back by train at an expense of about 10s. Ha could not believe that that motor car so hired was not used in the election. It seemed perfectly inare lible that for the first time in his life Arthur Peacock should go to the trouble of hiring a car for 50s. and not allow it to be used to bring up voters. Oa election day. Aqhur Peacock was apparently in charge of motor cars, and he stood outside the com- mittee room with cards and pap3rs in his hand. With regard to the pirt he took before the election day, a striking piece of evidence was given by Mr. Lacs, who successfully proved an alibi on Oztober 29th, because when Mr. fees saw Arthur Peaco3k the latter told him that for two days previously he had been over to War- rington at his brother's election. Taking all. the facts together, he was of opinion that Arthur Peacock was also an agent.

div.head: FRNNK ITUGFIES
div.p: FRNNK ITUGFIES

was also actively engaged canvassing the Roman Catholics, and be used the respondent's cirs only. Mr. Hughes, however, WAS a truthful witness and this case was properly not pressed by Mr. Dickens, but he was bound to say that if it had been pressed, nothing would have induced him to say that Frank Hughes was not an agent and most clearly proved to be so. He could only hope that Frank Hughes would not take part in any more contested elections. He had had a narrow escape, and he owed that first to his cwn truthfulness, and in the second place to the leniency of Mr. Dickens. He (the Commissioner) had carefully examined the evidence with regard to the following persons and he had no hesitation in holding them to be agents : Alcock, D ivies, Dumbell, Pemberton, Perry, Smart and Ambrose Wilkinson. Before proceeding to consider individual cases, he wished to draw attention to a practice which had time after time received the strongest condemnation of judges, and against which in the present election' he must enter a most emphatic protest. It was obvious that the petitioner in be ntture of things was compelled to prove his case chiefly by the evidence of persons drawn from the ranks of his opponent's quarters and it was not unnatural, in fact in many cases, it WAS necessary to obtain a signed state- ment from witnesses lest they should go back on information they had given. But the case was very different with the respondent. To rush in hot haste to a voter who had already signed a statement in favour of the petitioner and had thereby become one of his witnesses, and get him to .

div.head: SIGN A COUNTER-STATEMENT
div.p: SIGN A COUNTER-STATEMENT

completely denying all he had already sworn, was a Practice not to be defended. It conveyed the impression —sometimes perhaps An erroneous impression —that there was a determined attempt to stifle the inquiry by tampering with petitioner's witnesses and rendering valueless the evidence in his possession and it was much more likely to recoil upon the respondent than seriously to injure his opponent. Taking the charg(s seriatim he would first deal with
THE CHARGE OF BRIBERY BROUGHT AGAINST THE
RESPONDENT

himself. James Humphries, who was a man who drank heavily at times, said at 7.30 on the election day, he had a conversation with Ambrose Wilkinson near the Horse and Jockey. According to Humphries' version he was trying to get Rushworth in. Wilkinson went away, and came back in about three minutes, saying Humphries was wanted. The'' went into Longford-street and sa .v C mnoillor Cann'ngton talking to respondent. Respondent told Wilkinson to take Humphries to his house in West- street ; they went, and respondent followed. Humphries said that in the parlour respondent took the blue ribbon out of his coat put a red one in and gave him is. saying 'You know what to do." That was flatly denied by the respondent, and Wilkinson's story was that the blue ribbon was changed by him before they went into Long- ford-street. At all events, Wilkinson and Humphries went to the poll, and Humphries voted. Shortly after November 2nd there were rumours as to bribery, and the rumour at that time was that Wilkinson had given is. to llumphries. That got to the ears of the petitioner, and in the evening of November 9th, Rushworth and Haraphries went to the office of Messrs. Greenall, where Humphries signed a declaration saying he had been bribed with Is. by respondent. That visit was paid unquestionably between six and half-past six. In all probability Humphries was out of the place by half-past six. The evidence of Mr. Taylor and Mr. Jenkins was per- fectly plain and convincing on that point, and he accepted that as the time the declaration was signed. Now for the other side of, the story. Wood, the admitted agent of resporident, telephoned to Peacock that R ishworth had taken Humph-ries into Greenall's office, Humphries being drunk. Respondent at once came down, at.cl they and a man named Walsh watched for some time, and they all agreed that the time at. which they got there was between a quarter to eight and eight o'clock. Walsh and respondent swore that at' about a qtrarter past eight Hnmphries came out—Walsh said "drunk," respondent said "staggering drunk"— but he accepted the evidence entirely of Mr. Tayior and Mr. Jenkins that he was perfectly sober when he signed the declaration. It was not possible if the man had been in the drunken state described by the respond- ent that his condition could have 'escaped the netice of Messrs. Taylor and Jenkins. and he (the Commissioner) could not accept Mr. Madden's ingenious theory that it was a case of the superiority of mind over matter. What followed ? Walsh caught up Humphries, they went together up Winwick-road and they met Melia. They want into the British Tar, where Melia asked for three pints. Mr. Moffatt refiner; to serve any of them. it was suggested only because Humphries was drunk,but it was also stated that the other two having gone into the house with a drunken man and asked that lie should be servedos well as themselves,took umbrage at the refusal of Humphries and went out. He (the Commissioner) must confess that if that was the custom in Warrington it was a very curious one and did not commend itself to him as being at all likely. Walsh was an old publican and he avant, according to his own statement, into the British Tar with a Mall whom he knew to be drunk and had been drunk for some time,and was agree- able to drink with him. That convicted-Walsh of being a man of most careless habits and a man whi, on that statement alone, could hardly be trusted.

div.head: HORSE AND JOCKEY INCIDENT.
div.p: THE HORSE AND JOCKEY INCIDENT.

After loivin Ir. Aroffatt's public-house the men went in the direction of Humphries borne and when they reached the Horse and Jockey Humphries went in, leaving the others outside. P.C. Newey was outside in plain clothes, and a conversation took place, Walsh drawing his attention to the fact that Humphries was in the Jockey drunk. Then Peter Peacock came up and drew the officer's attention to the case and according to Newest said "If you can do Rishworth for permitting drunkenness the other case will fall through." Respon- dent denied that he said this, and stated that all he said to Newey was that he was to go in and do his duty. The officer went in according to his own statement, and maw Humphries there sober, and came out and told Peacock that was his opinion. But according to the others. Newey said he coul I not find Humphries in the place at all and that he must have gone. There was no reconciling those two statements. For a police officer to do what it, was alleged Newey had done.' was about

! the most foolish thing he could possibly have I done. There was absolutely no reason why any of the other men should not hive gone into the public-house and looked for themselves if Humphries was there. Newey mtde a report of .the case to his superior officer on the following day, and that bore out his own evidence. As regarded the stories ,of the respondent. and Newey, bearing in mind that he (the C3mmissioner) did not believe the story of the respondent that Ibinphrieß cane out of Oreenill's office druuk,and also that W.lstl was absolutely untrust- worthy on that point, he hid no hesitation in saying be believed the story of P.C. Newey. No attempt had been made to suggest that he was not a man of good character in the force and he (the Commissioner) was bound to hold that he was so. Walsh was an ex-publican, he had been with this alleged drunken man- in the British Tar, he saw him as far as the Horse and Jockey according to his own statement not attempting to lead him as the man could walk without aid, and yet when he (the Commissioner) asked him why he did not follow Ifumphries into the Horse and Jockey, and fetch him out, his answer was that he did not see why he should do anything of the lcinJ, and that he had been lugging him along and was sick of it. That was an absolute contradiction of his own evidence. Walsh had

div.head: TOLD MONSTROUS UNTRUTHS
div.p: TOLD MONSTROUS UNTRUTHS

in the witnesq box, and he must. reject his evidence as worthless. He (the Commissioner) accepted the story laid before him on behalf of the petitioner as to what happened on November 9th. Oa November 10th the respondent and his friends, wishing to counteract the declaration signed by Humphries, followed him with the object in which they succeeded of getting him to sign a second declaration entirely contradicting the other one. It was rather curious that when, according to respondent's case, Humphries, who had been at work until lite in the afternoon, was hopelessly drank on November 9th, on the next evening, when there was no evidence that he had been at work, he was perfectly sober. He did not mike much of it, but there was the fact. The second declaration, which was found after some trouble was, to his mind,
ABSURD ON' TB FAC9 OF IT

As regarded Mr. %Wight, who took it, there was nat the faintest ground for suspecting the absolute truth of every word he said. He acceptied Mr. Wright's evidence that Humphries was not drunk when he signed the second declaration, but llnmphries was in charge of a number of men, including his Own brother, who, he was afraid had been looking him up, and recollections of these witnesses as to the contents of the declaration were conflicting. Aecording to one of then he said he actually signed a declaration in Messrs. Greenall's office that Rushworth had offered him £l5 for saying respond- ent had given him Is. It was utterly ridiculous to suppose he said anything of the kind, and no doubt the declaration he signed before Mr. Wright embodied in substance what he did say. It was to be remarked that the second declaration had been written down by Peacock himself before they went Mr. Wright at all. If he (the Commissioner) was to put one declaration against the other, he bad no hesitation in saying he believed the one signed on the 9th as against the one signed on the Plth. Dealing with the events of the election day, the CJIII- missioner said the truth of the allegation against the responder.t depended upon whether Horn/Aries was ever in Peacock's house at all, and they had only his direct evidence that ho was. It was curious that Homphries brought on the. spot in that house not only Peter Peacock and Ambrose Wilkinson but also a lady. They did not know who she was, hut there was undoubtedly a lady in the house who had not been accounted for. Ambrose Wilkinson ',said it was he who changed Humphries' ribbon,but he (the Commissioner) found the

div.head: STORY DIFFICULT TO CREDIT
div.p: STORY DIFFICULT TO CREDIT

----- for this reason : Humphries was not asked a word about it in cros:-examination, and it was so material that he did not suppose it possible thlt counsel would have failed to question him on such a paint. It had been remarked that nothing about the exchange of the ribbon could have been known, so far as he could judge, at the time when Ambrose Wilkinson went t 3 the respondent's house to ask what the charge against him was, and it looked very much as if the contention of Nfr. Dickens had a great deal in it—that the story of the exchange of the ribbon by Wilkinson was made up after Hutuphries had given his evidence. Of course, that was a very serious charge to make, but it w.is no less a charge th It was to be investigated, and he had studied to see if he could come to a definite conclusion from any of the surrounding circumstances or any of the other witnesses. It was only on the Wednes- day before thu trial, according to Wilkinson's story, that anything was said . about the ribbon, but he (the Commissioner) was afraid there was only too much ground to suppose that nothing could have been said about it then, though of course, it was possible that a man like Humphries might have said something about it in a drunken state, but they had no evidence as to where the knowledge of the exchange of ribbons cune from before Humphries got into the box. It was in favour to some extent of the resnondent's account that C inneilfor Cunnineton sup- ported the 'statement that Humphries and Wilkinson passed by on the other side of the street on the election moraine, but while he had not the slightest doubt that Councillor Cunnington was giving a perfectly accurate version, his evidence did not dispose ot the wiestion, because it was a singular fact that. respondent walked away alone and went back to his house in West-street, for some sandwiches. The suggestion was that about that time lie took Humphries into a room and gave him a bribe. In the first place it did seem inherently improbable that a person in the position of respondent would have done such a thing because he ran the risk of being seen. On the other hand, Humphries, in making a false charge a ainst the respondent, could easily have done it without alleging it took place under such circumstances as really gave him away at the hands or the opposite party whenever they chose to contra- dict him. To his mind a great deal depended upon the route taken by Humphries and Wilkinson on the way to the polling booth. They might have turned out of Longford-street into Hale-street, at the corner of which was the respondent's home and thence gone along West-street and Dudley-street. or they migbt have gone along Earl-street and so into Dudley- street. it had been remarked that West-street and Dudley-street were in a direct line. There was only one small piece of evidence bearing on the point. and that was the evidence of Roden, who lived in Dudley-street and who on going out of his house at 7.50 on the election morning saw Humphries and Wilkinson turn the corner of Dudley-street into Orford-lane. He could not say whether they turned out of Earl-street into Dudley-street or whether they came straight down from West-street. If there had been evidence that Wilkinson and Humphries went straight into Dudley-street from Wust-street, the inference he would have drawn would have been irresistible—that they were coming from the resp-mdent's house. floweveri there was no evidence to that effect. Therefore he bed to consider which side a very slight balance of evidence, in his opinion, must incline to. It was obvious if the charge sug- gested aeainst Hr. Peter Peacock was proved, he had been guilty of a fearful crime. The suggested con- spiracy between himself and Wilkinson was so terrible and, if it was true, the perjury used to support that case was so shocking that he hesitated to come to the conclusion that either of them could be guilty. He therefore gave them the benefit of the doubt, and he

POUND THIS Cl/ARGE NOT PROVED, but the respondent though he escaped from this charge did not escane with honour or on the strength of his own case. He held the charge not proved by reason of the absence of one or two links in the chain of evidence ngainst him, and had Humphries been a man of irreproachable character, instead of the poor unhappy drunkard he was, the decision might well have been the other way. Dealing with • THE CASE OF ELSIE WILKINSON the Cammissioner said it had given him more personal anxiety than any ho had had before him. One could not help btrit feel that, for a girl not yet 17 years old to be mixed up in such a case was simply Lamentable. Although one ought not to allow a feel- inr! of sentiment to influence him he had endeavoured to do his utmost to find a way consistent with the evidence of exculpating Elsie Wilkinson from the cherge brought against her. The charge was that she went to Mrs. Lawrinsou's in Foster-street at two o'clock on polling day and gave her 61. in the lobby, came out and took her to the polling booth in a motor car. The same night Mr.Gillen,hrother-in=law to the respondent, went to Mrs. Lawrinson's house and asked if she had had any money. She denied it. Subsequently she made a declaration in the presence of Mr. Jenkins and Mr. Taylor to the effect that she received 6d. from Elsie Wilkinson, and she adhered to that in the witness box. It was true, in pursuance of that very ill-advised course of obtaining a contradictory statement, Mr. Peter Pea Cock, Mr. Wright and others went to her house to endeavour to get to sign a statement but she refused and with the exception of what she said to Mr. Gillen on the night of the poll, she had stuck to her story the whole way through. Elsie Wilkinson denied it abso- lutely, and the question was whether there was suffi- cient corroboration on the pin of the four women standing in Melville-street, who said they saw Elsie Wilkinson go into the kitchen. She denied that she went beyond the lobby and, seeing she was so busily engaged that day, that was just possible and he would give her the benefit of the dotrbt on that point which in any event was not very material as the bribery was alleged to 'have taken place in the lobby Three of the witnesses spoke to the suspicious move- ment made by Elsie Wilkinson and he was bound to say that the evidence of Mrs. Davies seemed very strong. He was not so impressed with t le evidence of Mrs. Gleave and Mrs. Gregory. As to whether it was possible to see into the lobby from where the women were standing, he had paid four visits to the ward to test the matter, but such was his perplexity that he thought he must decide the question as to where the motor car was standing at .the time. The evidence on that was conflicting but he thought it was reasonable to hold that the car went up the left hand side of Melville-street, turned round as Elsie Wilkinson described,and backed until it stood in front, of the front, door of Mrs. Lawrinson's house. That would be a reasonable place to pull up, and he thought that from the position where the women were standing the car would have been in front of the door. It was quite possible that the position of the car hindred them from having a full view of what was going on inside and therefore, he should give Elsie Wilkinson the benefit of the doubt.. He wished to give Elsie Wilkinson a word of advice. Contested elections wete not matters for

young girls or grown-up women to interfere with, and he trusted th'it. her first app.arance as agent in an election would be her last, and that her experience would act as a warning to her in future. Tue Cim- missioner then dealt with the case of
SULAM ELLEN lIADCROFT.

who was alleged to have received sixpence from 11Irs. Silcock on returning from the poll. A terrible scene occurred on the second day of toe trial. Sie made a statement of the simplest kind as to 6.1. having been given her and then she came to the box and denied it absolutely. They had not the advantage of her corrected statement, but he (the Commissioner) formed a strong opinion the moment the witness began to give her evidence on the important point that she was simply denying what doe knew to be true. She; took up the defined attitude of a person who had been tampered with and who had come prepared to say positively that all she had slid before was false. For the greater part of two days she hal been in the room in which the respondent's witnesses were accommodated. Mrs. Silcock had keen there, and it was admitted that Hadoroft spoke to her. H 3 did not infer that Mrs. Silcock was the person who got her to come into Court to deny the statement which had been made, but that Hadcroft was tampered with in the .room was a eon- elusion which he thought anyone who exercised ' commonsense was bound to draw. Her subsequent statement consisted of two assertions only in 'answer to questions from him (the Commissioner)--first, that she bad received sixpence, an,' secondly that the person who gave it to her was Mrs. SAcock. It was, of course, open to suggestion that she was not in a fit state to make a statement at all, but on that point he (the Com- missioner) must exercise his own judgment. He scrutinised her narrowly and he had not the faintest doubt that the evidence she gave when she came back into the Court was absolutely true. He could not accept Mrs. Slcock's denial and he was bound, there- fore, to find that the case had beep proved. With regard to

div.head: CASE OF SARAH HOUGHTOY,
div.p: THE CASE OF SARAH HOUGHTOY,

that was a case in which a charge was made against Mrs. Si!cock of having made a promise of a drink on the way to th..poll for voting for the respondent. He would sad no more about the case than this—that it was a story not likely to have been invented. It bore the impress of truth upon it. and unless he was prepired to hold digt, other witnesses for the petitioner had deliber- ately got up a false story he was bound to accept her evidence. The denial of Mrs. Silcock was tinged with the impossibility of placing credence on her story with regard to th 3 Hadcroft case and he must hold thit the case had been proved. He wac: not going to refer to lnSti.ins. CASE

It would make matters too long to do so, because IL was not a case of ,direct bribery, and he only mentioned the matter to show that he had not entirely forgotten it. If the evidence of Alnrshall was accepted it went far to attack the credit of the reap mdont. He would say no more about that matter. He now came to the

CHARGES AGAINST ARTHUR PEACOCK. First be would take Richard Bailey's case. The story was that he was in the Soldier's Returin jt•st after the close of the poll. He went nut and We saw Mr. Arthur Peacock in Winwick-road. He asked him for the price of a pint of beer for himself and his vat and Arthur Peacock said he did not think he had any money, but he put his hand in his pocket and panel out two three- penny bits and gave them to Bailey. This charge was really admitted. Peacock admitted that be gave some- thing, but he did not know how much—whether it was a sixpence or two threepenny pieces—but he admitted that a man he never knew before came up to him after the close of the poll and asked him for money, which he gave to him. His explanation was curious—" Per- haps I might have thought that Bliley looked as if he needed it.' It was hardly likely at that time that litiley would look as if he wanted it, or that a mere charitable feeling tempted him to give the six- pence. That was well within the principle on which the law of bribery rested, and as regarded that charge he lied no hesitation in saying that it was made out. There was another charge which incidentally •arose out of that visit to the S diners' Return-liter the close of the poll, and that was the charge that Arthur Peacock treated Bailey and *other persons unknown to seven or eight pints of beer. What he (the speaker) had to say about that was that he did not consider that the evidence was sufficient to support the charge, and that' the case was not proved. Then there was the case in which Alcock was charged with having treated Richard Bailey to a pint of beer on the afternoon of the poll. Alcock was in Silver-street when B tiley came up. They had been speaking about the election before that,and Bailey said he had voted and asked Aloock to lend him a shilling until the next club night. Alcock said he had no change and asked Bailey to. go into the Red Lion. They went there together, along with another man named Narroway, and Alcock paid for drinks with half- a crown out of which he gave B'a'iley 91d., and told him he would owe him a shilling. Ft was clear that Alcock had worked hard for Peacock' ell day long and was an agent, end it was a strange commentary on his conduct that Bailey had never borrowed a single halfpenny from him before or after that day. Alcock said that the shilling was a loan and that he expected to be paid back some day, but he had to admit that he and Narroway left the Unicorn, leaving Bailey, and that he expected he would drink the 91d. before he came away. In his (the Commissioner's) judgment the story of the loan was more or leis of an after-thought and it was a clear case of Creating. With regard to

GEORGE JAMES COOPER there were chargesbf both bribery and treating. He did not think the evidence of tho promise was quite sufficiently satisfActory hut he thrmght a case of treat- ing had been proved. He did not think it was any answer to the evidence to suggest that it was a mere social glass. It was, in fact, a case of treating after Cooper had voted, but the bribery charge would fall through. The

div.head: CASE OF FISHER
div.p: CASE OF FISHER

I wasn very difficult one. Fisher testified to a conversa- tion about 1 30 in which Wood said something about a pint. At 7.30 he saw Wood again in Silver-street and lasked him where his pint was and Wood said "I will see you get it.." Wood, however, was not able to go ; himself and he told a friend of his to take Fisher into the UnTdorn and give him his drink. Wood denied that but it was admitted that while Wood was busy, James Rose took Risber into the Unicornand stood him a pint. Rose said" I saw he wanted a pint "all then be made , the extraordinary admission that he never bad a drink with him before. Why Rose should choose on election day to stand drink to a man he had never drunk with before,was to his (thespeaker's)mind incomprehensible. .He could not doubt that Rose went as the agent of i Wood, who was too busy to go himself, and stood the . drink to Fisher, and that case was clearly proved. With I regard to the case of

div.head: EDWARD GLEAVE
div.p: EDWARD GLEAVE

the man admittedly had a-t-i.e;;i-five drinks by nine o'clock in the morning and be thought it was reasonable to suppose that he was not in a condition at the time when the conversation took place, to make it likely that his evidence could be relied upon. Therefore he dismissed Gleave's case. Dealing with the case of

THOMAS KNIGHT, the Commissioner said that before the election a visit was paid to him by John Melia, his father-in-law, Alf Wood, and John Williams and they endeavoured to get this strong Tory to vote for Peaco7.k. It was suggested that the men left together and that in a short time Melia returned with a bottle of beer, the inference being that Wood had supplied him with drink or money to get it. Melia, however, said he left half an hour after the others and did not see them again that

4ght. Taken by itself, that did not seem a strong case, hit unfortunately one could not leave out what I happened on a subsequent Sunday when Knight went to I Melia's and Wood came to him and was alleged to have said "Don't press the charge against me. I have a wife and rive children. If they find me out it means twelve months." That some such conversation took place was certain, because it, was admitted by Wood himself. Wood spoke of the fear he was in and mentioned some story about ducks, but he (the Commissioner) could not believe that that story had anything to do with it. The words alleged to hive been spoken by Wood were so curiously like those alleged to have been spoken by others implicated in charges, that he drew the conclusion that they referred to the charge of bribing Knight with a bottle of beer, and that charge was in his judgment proved. With regard to the charge against Dimbell, he thought there was not sufficient 'evidence to support it. Ile would say no more than that the charge was not proved. He now came to the

ILAST CIIARGE OF BRIBERY, thatagainst Sinart,who was bald to have bribed Thomas Jones, with p remise of payment and food for voting. The evidence of Jones himself had not proved the case. He raid Abraham Smart came to his front door and shouted "Jump up, dad,it will be all right" and,according to him, that was all the convers Won. Bat Mrs. Brace- girdle who lived-in the same house, was standing close by and heard the conversation. Apparently she did not wish to bring it out, and iti was only when she was shown her previous statement that the full facts came out. Her statement was that S nart said " Come on and you will hive a good feed. You will get your belly full." Jones had told her she could not hear Smart say it and therefore she accepted it as a contradiction. He (the Commissioner) could not believe her story was invented. It was not the sort of expression sle would have invented and was afraid he could do nothing but credit her statment and find the case also proved. The other case was against Davies and Pemberton, who were charged as well as Arthur Peacock ' with treating certain voters in the ward at the Soldiers' Return on October 23th. He could only say that Arthur Peacock had proved conclusively an alibi, and he dismissed that at once. D ivies and Pemberton, were, however, there and Davies had proved the am agiinst himself. div.head: HONEST AND STR AI C HTFORWATt D WITNESS
div.p: HONEST AND STR AI C HTFORWATt D WITNESS

and his only explanation for treating was that he had , had a bet, and thus felt justified in treating people. If ' people wonld pers:st in treating others who might be voters at election time, it really did not matter what the sources of the money were, whether from the , bankers or from betting a few shillings. It was equally treating and he must find that the charge was proved against Davies, but he did not think the evidence was sufficient against Pemberton. lie was extremely sorry to find the charge against Davies proved, because he was to his mind, one of the most honest witnesses they had had during the whole of the inquiry. Tnerefore, though he was obliged to name Davies, be hoped no serious consequences would follow. Ile bad now dealt with the whole of the charges on which evidence had been offered and , TUE RESULT OF THE INQUIRY 'was that he found that the respondent was not legally elected and his election was void, on the grounds of bribery and treating on the part of his agents, and it would be his dtey to certify to his Majesty's judges to that effegt. Mere only remained the question as to the extent to which corrupt practices had been indulged in. Whatever his suspicions might be, no evidence had been adduced which would justify his coming to an adverse conclusion,and his report would be that corrupt practices did not extensively prevail at theelection. Mr. Swift said the C mimistioner had not mentioned one case—that of GleAve being treated by Alfred Wood. The CJIII missioner : I dismiss the whole of the cases of Gleave.

Mr. Madden: There is the charge of bribery against George Henry Perry. The Commissioner: Dismissed. NO CY3r.3 A-313 P3ll, BY TH:?, rITiONErt. Mr. Swift said as to the matter of costs, he was instructed on behalf of Mr. Rushworth not be ask for any order for his costs against the respondent. Mr. Rushworth had presented this petition with the object of showing to the electors of Warrington that corrup- tion which he alleged had taken place, must not be allowed in municipal elections, and a ith the object of showing that a seat won in this way could not be retained. Having done that, he had no desire to be vindictive so faras concerned punishing the respondent, by asking for an order for costs against him. He did not ask for any costs for the petitioner. There were other costs which might naturally fall upon the responient, bat abut those he would'sAy alythin3.
MR DIC CEN3 AND 11318 I'RT DAVIE 3.

Mr. Svift said there was one other matter, and that was in regard to Harbert Davies. Mr. Dickens instructed him to mention the matter to the C mmissioner on his behalf and he (Mr, S "gift) was encouraged to do so by the remtrks of the C)mmissioner. Mr. Dickens asked him to point out tint Herbert D Ivies had given his evidence perfectly straightforwardly in the box as to the facts, and he therefore asked the Commissioner to !titre him a certificate of indemnity. The Claimissioner : Ha his told the truth in the box.

Mr. S.vift : Mr. Dickens would personally like to ask that a cartilicite of indernity be given to Davies. The Commissioner: I will bear that in mind. Mr. Nltdden : I wiih to ask for a certificlte of indemnity on behalf of Arthur Pocock. I think he was truthful in the box too. •

The Commissioner said that before he mole a report to the judges of the witnesses convicted by him of the charges Against then, notice must be given to show cause why they should not be reported. They must be at the C mrt by a quarter past ten the next morning to show cause why they should not be reported.

div.head: QUESHON OF C33TS.
div.p: QUESHON OF C33TS.

. - - Mr. Byrn') s 'id th 3 Public Prosecutor hid instructed him to dra v the C.nurnissioner's attention to Secti on 101, &b-section 2, of the C)rrupt Practices Act with reference to the costs which would ultimately fall upon the borough, on the grounds th tt he had cons derable discretion with regard to them and might make an order for their re-imbursement. Toe C.)mmissioner :nid he had not found the respondent personally guilty and he had therefore no power to comply with the request. In answer to Hr. Madden, the Commissioner said that with regard-to the costs on the borough, be would let them follow the ordinary course and not make an order for them to be paid by anybody else. Mr. Madden said they had had a good fight. So far as Mr. Rushworth and Mr. Peacock were concerned, he thought their personal relationships were most cordial, and on behalf of Mr. Peacook be thanked the other side for the generous and he might say extremely friendly manner in which they had acted in the question of costs. On behalf of those he represented he thanked them for the generous conduct in not asking for costs in this matter. He felt that this was a very pleasant ending to the long contest. _
The' Commissioner : I only hope \Varrington will not have another election petition for many years to come.
Mr. Afadden : I don't know that I can quite agree with that. (Laughter). The proceedings :then closed.

div.head: INDEMNITY CERTIFICATES FOR WITNESSES.
div.p: INDEMNITY CERTIFICATES FOR WITNESSES.
Three Refused.

The election Court assembled for the last time on Tuesday morning when the Commissioner heard appli- cations for indemnity certificates on behalf of those persons concerned in the charges which he had held to be proved. _ _ _
Mr. Rees represented Wood, Alcock, Arthur Peacock, Mrs. Silcock, Smart and Davies. Mr. Byrne was present in the interests of the Public Prosecutor. A CERTIFICATE FOR MR. A. PEACOCLi.

The first case taken was that of Arthur Peacock. Mr. Rees pointed out that an alibi had been proved in the treating and that was out of the inquiry. The only point proved was with regard to two threepenny bits, and Arthur-Peacock in the witress box said it was most likely he did give 6d. or two threepenny bits. He told the truth absolutely in regard to that matter. As regarded the motor car no charge had been made.

The Commissioner said he ;-v. as bound to report Mr. Peacock for bribery hut he could grant a certificate which would protect him from any further proceedings. He believed Mr. Peacock told the truth-in the witness hex, and although he could not acquit him of very serious misconduct during the election he would grant him a certificate.
MRS. SILCOCK REFUSED.
Mr. Rees said Mrs. Si!cock's sister was in attendance to prove that she was unwell during the fortnight pre- ceding the election.

The Con3rnissioner said it wns necessary to call that evidence, as he bad found Mrs. Silcock committed bribery and he would have to report her. Mr. Rees submitted that the Commissioner's decision in the Hadcroft.case was an inference from the facts, and that Mrs. Silcock did tell the truth from her point of view.

The Commissioner said that unfortunately be could not possibly take the view that Mrs. Silcock told the truth in the witness box. Ile could not grant a certifi- cate, but he might say candidly that his view was that it was not likely that in her case any further proceedings would be taken.

div.head: CERTIFICATE FOR ALCOCK.
div.p: CERTIFICATE FOR ALCOCK.

With regard toiWilliam Rylands Alcock, Mr. Rees raid there was a conflict of evidence. A man named Bailey raid he owed Alcock 21d., and Alcock said Bailey owed Is. Alcock paid for a pint of beer and gave Bailey 91d. change, making the Is. The point which affected the Commissioner's judgment was that Peacock had never stood Bailey a drink before or since and that the money had not been repaid. He (Mr. Rees)
submitted that Alcock told the truth and the Com- midsioner inferred something which upheld the charge of bribery • . _ _

The Commissioner said he came there prepared to refuse Alcock. He was not clear that this was a case in which he might not reasonably grant a certific-tte,and on the whole he did not think any harm would be done by it. It was rather a dangeroui thing to pat m iney down in a public-house on election day. Tne certificate was granted. WOOD REFUSED IN TWO CASES.

Mr. Rees said Vier° were several cases against Alfred Wood. In the case of Fisher, it was quite clear Rose stood the drink. and Rose aid not allege he receivei anything from Wood. Rose was not a worker in the election. Wood did not tell any untruth about the facts, lie worked all day in the election, seeing hundreds of men, and it was impossible for Ilia) to rememberaccarately what conversation took place with each man. If his recollection differed from Fisher's he (Mr. Rees) urged that he should not in any way be hurt in consequence. As regarded Knight he asked the Commissioner to believe Wood was speaking the truth as he had admitted there was a dispute and he said something about his wife and children. In the case of Cooper there was no denial of the fact that Wood stood him a drink. Wood was an honest witness, and what he said bore the impress of truth in every case. It was an inference drawn from the fact that was against him and not the fact itself.

The Commissioner said as regarded George James Cooper be would grant Wood a certificate, but he could not grant him a certificate in the case of Fisher or Kuight. He would leave that to the Public Prosecutor to decid...

div.head: WARNTNG.
div.p: A WARNTNG.
11fr. Rees mentioned the case of lferbert Davies, The Commissioner : You need not trouble about him. _

DAvies wits called foto the box and the Con-ii-ni;;Co.;;I: said he WAS glad to be able to grant him a certificate because he believed he told the truth in the witness- box. lie must, however, warn him not to treat his friend!, at election time again. D ivies : I will see it does not happen again. The Commissioner: You won't hear any more of this.

div.head: ABRAHANI SMART REFUSED.
div.p: ABRAHANI SMART REFUSED.

Mr. Rees in asking for a certificate for Abraham Smart pointed out that it was admitted there was a conversation and the conflict was between the recollec- tion of Mrs. Bracegirdle and the other witnessea. S:nart was a man who from eight o'clock in the morning until eight o'clock at night on the day of the poll went about seeing voters in different parts of the-ward, and it was hard for him to suggest that because he could not recollect the conversation which took place he was un- truth ful.He would have hundreds of conversations during the day. Something was said ah3ut feeding and having a" belly full," but it was more in the nature of a jocular conversation than anything else and it was construed into one of bribery. The point that day was whether Smart, having regard to what ho did on the day of the election, made a truthful statement to the Commissioner when he was in the box. He (Mr. Rees) contended that Smart did make a truthful statement to the best of his recollection.

The Commissioner said Mr. fleas bad put the case very admiraily and very ingeniously, but he was afraid that if his suggestion were carried into effect it would mean th .t nearly everybody doing that sort of thing on the day of an election would get oft and it would he impossible to find anyone guilty. Al the same time he w.ts not going to say that this was a serious case. Ile did not take that view of it, but a conversation about a good meal and a "belly full" was a sort of thing one would not be likely to forget. lie did not think Smart could possibly have forgotten a suggession like that which had been named. lie could not give him a certifi- cate. He must not be absurdly lenient in these cases ; he must draw the line somewhere.
Mr. Rees r That is my last case. The Commissioner : You have done very well; you have turned me round in one case.
MORE (I!cjiT(FICATES O1ANI7g1),

To the ch.se of George James C3op3r, the missioner said Cooper had allowed himself to be treated to a glaFs of whisky, but as he had told the truth he would have a certificate. Persons who accepted were guilty of bribery and treating just the same as those who gave.

The Commissioner addressed Albert Fisher in similar terms, and granted him a certificate. It was stated that Sarah Ellen fiadcroft wai too unwell to attend, but her brother was present: The Commissioner: I shall dispense with her attend- ance. lam convinced that in answer to my question at the last moment she did tell the truth, and therefore she is entitled to the certific tte which I shall give her. Addres.ing Richard Bailey, the Commissioner said : You did a very impudent thing at the election. You have been tribed without the slightest doubt. Do not do it again in another election, or it may go hard with you. I think you told the truth in the box, so I shall give you a certificate.

- When l'hornas Knight was ',ailed the Commissioner sad : You did a more stupid thing than a wicked thing, but you brought yourself within the law. You accepted what I am bound to hold was a bribe, hut you told the truth about it, and I shall give youacertificato

div.head: FURTHER PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: FURTHER PROCEEDINGS.
Mr. Byrne asked the Commissioner if be had any directions to give as to any further proceedings against persons concerned in the ease.
- The Commissioner : I have no directions whatever to give you. I will leave you with an entirely free hand.
THE DOCUMENTS.
On the question of the documents produced in tl,e case, Mr. Byrne raid that there was only one he wished to be retained and that was the statement of Sarbh Ellen lialcroft. •
'rhe Commissioner directed the Registrar to retain it.
THE COST TO THE TOWN.

Mr. Byrne raised the question as to whether it was possible under certain circumstances for the C nn- missioner to order the costs of the Public Prosecutor or some equivalPnt Fie re-imbursed to the Corporation. Tne Commissioner : lio.v may times in the course of your experience have you known that to be done? Mr. Byrne: I have never known it to be done. The Commissioner: I think there are one or two cases in which it has been done, but I don't propose to do it, here.

div.head: COMMISSIONER'S COMPLIMENTS.
div.p: COMMISSIONER'S COMPLIMENTS.

The Commissioner : The only thing I have to say before we finally rise is that I wish to convey my thanks to the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), and the Deputy-Town Clerk (Mr. A. I'. Holloway) for the admirable arrange- ments they have made for the reception of this Com- mission. t oiling could have been better done than him been done here. Really the way in which the proceedings have been arranged is a pattern to the country. I also wish to thank the Chief Constable(Mr. Nichol Is) for the admirable arrangements he has made for the Court. ram certain that no election inquiry lasting twelve days has ever been conducted with the order and decorum with which this one has and that is largely due to the arrangements of the Chief Constable. Mr. Byrne: If I may respectfully say so, I subscribe most cordially to what you say. Mr. Rees : r join in thanking the Mayor, the Town Clerk, and the-Deputy Town Clerk for their courtesy and hospitality. We all hope that the people of Warrington will settle down in unity, and carry on the good government of the town, that enmities may cease and good fellowship prevail. (Hear, hear.)
