The great Warrington election TILE GREAT petition, after a hearing PETITION. extending over twelve days and involving the expendi- ture of a huge sum of money—and much of it public money—ehas resulted in a victory for the petitioner and his party. Bat it is a hollow and empty victory,and one on which the Conservatives cannot pride themselves. Tuey have unseated Mr, Peter Peacock and obtained a verdict that the election of November last was null and void. S) far they succeeded. Bat what does it all mean? D .e; any elector in Wirrin4ton believe that the party which finds so many aims in common with the debasing , liquor interest, was animated in this petition solely by the desire to wash out the horrid stains of bribery and treating in a ward electioe ? If we thought that the Conservatives of Warrington were legitimately ensconced on such a high pedestal we should unhesitatingly applaud them, for no one can con- tend with any show of reason or decency that the procuring of votes by the offering of sixpence here and a pint of beer _there is anything but repre- hensible and demoralising. The fieding of the Commissioner was that there had been a certain amount of bribery and treating by the agents of Mr. Peacock, and that therefore he had not been legally.elected. The Commissioner also exoressed the opinion that" corrupt practices did not exten- sively prevail at the election." As a matter of fact the sum total of the expenditure on brib3ry and treating which the petitioners were able to prove could be covered ny a five-shilling piece. The one 'personal charge of bribery ageinso Mr. Peaeock—the Humphries ewe—failed. We have therefore the pretty spectacle of something like £3,000 being spent to prove five shillingsworth of bribory and treating. It reminds us of the labour of the mountain to produce a—mouse.

There . are certain other WHY WAE THE SEAT facts in the case which NuT CLAIMED? deserve to be dragged into the light of day.- Toe petitioner has unseated his onpoQent, but he has not won the seat. Why? B cause he 11 n d his friends did not claim the seat, as they could have done. Would they have got it? Tnat is another cinestion, and a very significant one. By claiming the seat as well as petitioning against the return of Mr. Peacock, the petitioning side would have laid themselves open to recriminatory charges from the other side. This, they doubtless considered to be an ordeal which had better he avoided. Certain agents of the respondent might also have been found guilty of indiscreet treating, and even bribery. A. man is at the mercy of his agents in these matters, and no one can be expected to believe that all the corrupt practice is on the side of the Libetal party. Bribery and treating arise fro-n oppirtunity, and the oppor- tunity is dependent on the means. ISI)w, which side possesses the means in Warrington ? Mr. Peacock has 103 t his seat, hut the Conserve tive have not won it. Marecv )r, we a ) not believe that they can !
There is another point. PAYIWG TI Tht) Cmservatives, PIPER. bringing this petition,

chose the most expansive and cumbrous method of securing their end. They could have laid their charges before a Judge of Assize, as was done in the Ghngh case, instead of causing a C iurt to be set up in Wirrington, which will, we are informed, cost the ratepiyers some- thing like £1,030 —an ex`,ra penny on the rates. By going to the Assizis, the cost to the town would have been it& iitesimal. Wny this wanton disregard for the public puree ? o:ford Ward might have been purged without the whole town having to pay for tt. Tin .ConservAtive party made a big mistake when they saddled the rate- payers with such a burden in order to unseat Mr. Peacock. We can only find one excuse for them. Possibly they realised that unless the personal charge against the respondent was proved, he would not have been unseated by a Judge of ASS'Zi. The irresponsible agents who bribed and treated wou'd have had to appear as defendants and "stand their own corner" —to use a collo- ipialism. Apparently the intention was to unseat Mr. Peacock—this m irked man who had defied the brewe-y monopoly —c ,st what it might. And it has cost us a peony in the p lurid ! . We hope the public will appreciate the privilege of paying.

Much has been said and THE NURSING written in praise of the ASSOCIATION. district nurses but it is i mrssible to exaggerate the value of the work which they do for the poorer classes of Warrington. When sickness casts its shadow over lowly abodes where through ignorance or straitened circumstances the sufferer is apt to be neglected, the nurses by their kindly and efficient ministrations effect a transibrmation which brightens the surroundings of the sick room and brings comfort to the patient. Lllce most deserving institutions the Warrington Astrict Nursing Association has had a difficulty in making ends meet, but a determined efiert is now being made to place it on a sound financial. basis and to increase interest in its work In another column we publish a substantial list of subscriptions raceived in response to the thnely appeal of the hon. treasurer (Mr. Henry R eberts). There is, however, still plenty of opportunity for those who desire to have a share in relieving this excellent institution from financial erabarrasinent. In Mr. R therts' appeal, issued in December, it was pointed out that on the present basis, the expenditure exceeds the income by nearly £l2O per annum, in addition to which, each year several subscribers are lost through removals or other causes, while recently some subscripions have been withdrawn .for the purpose of maintaining nurses in adj icent districts. Tne needs of the Association are pester than ever, and unless the funds are idcreased the nursing staff must be reduced before long, or special appeals will have to be made periodically for the purpose of clearing off accumulated deficits. Neither course would, of course, be desirable, and we believe the public of Warrington have snffi•clent generosity to ensure Ihat the institu'ion shall not be hampered for want of subFcriptions. Parents all over the c.ivatry' RACING PJlt BJIN. will be interested in the

opinions gathered by Mr. Hubert Farmer, an old 114rrovian, from five eminent physicians on the Eubj int of long-listance racing for boys. No one who has even competed in a mile race will contest the assertion that the strain is very heavy. For boys of a growing age it is necessarily a much greater trial than for men When the distance is increased beyond the mile the strain become muith greater. Toe five doctots whom Mr. Farmer has consulted are of opinion that no boys under nineteen years should be permitted to compete in races ex2eeding 8 mile in tength. The reasons are perfectly obvious. The tremendous strain of continuous running for long distances is calculated to cause permanent injury to the heart and other organs. Not only is this so in regard to running. Ther3 are other sports which entail equal strain and similiar consequence 3. It would be interest. ing to know, for instance, how many who have achieved the distinction of a University Boatrace in recent years have suffered aftErwards from the killing strain of the last stretch. *Public school- masters have a duty to the parents to perform in regard to the health of the boys in their charge They will do well t 3 take notice of what is said by these doctors. Excessive physical training of all kinds should be avoided. Boys are the better an being hardened, but there are limits. There is for evil of physical, as well as of mental, "cramming.'

* * * Owing to the peculiarity of ths law as to furnishing the particulars of charges, the respondent in the election petition case had only five days in which to prepare his defence. Examiner Saturday, February 20, 1909. NOTES AND NOTIONS.

A word of caution is necessary (says the " Anti- Socialisnto restrain the optimists who are continually announcing the destruction of Socialism, and are often confounded by its ressurrection. We must not attach too much importance to Socialist quarrels. The Socialists have been quarrelling incessantly for over twenty years, and the mores they have quarrelled the more the movement has prospered. Socialism is one of those organisms which propagate themselves by fissure.

* * * Everybody who is anybody in the Liberal Party (says the Westminster Gazette) seemed to be present at the reception at the Admiralty on Monday night, and the occasion was a brilliant success. Mrs. McKenna, in pale blue velvet, played the part of hostess charmingly amid surroundings which she has almost transformed since her marriage. Probably no lady so young has ever been hostess on so importgot a political occasion, but there was no suggestion of want of experience in the grace with which "Mrs. McKenna received the great company of her guests. * * *

An anecdote of Charles Darwin, whose centenary was celebrated yesterday week, shows convincingly how deep was his passion for natural history. In his youth, it is said, when entomology attracted him most, he was searching in an old tree trunk for "tt somewhat rare beetle. He found one, and just as he grasped it a second of the same species appeared. Both the naturalist's hands were occupied, but he could not let slip the chance of so great a capture. So he put the first beetle in his mouth and triumphantly seized the other. We have never heard of anyone else who suffered from entomology in so acute a form.

* * * The work I have been able to do in my lifetime has been proportionate to my abstinence fro:n alcoholic drink.—Mr. John Burns. The day may come when the whole of England, from north to south, from east to west, will be united in one great Roman Catholic Confederation, prepared to act with decision and with energy whenever the Roman Catholic Church has to be defended.— Ardtbishop Bourne.

Mr. Justice Walton recalled some pleasant memories of his native country at a meeting of the Association of Lancastrians in London which was held on Monday evening. Strangers who rushed into Lancashire by Runcorn and Widnes and St. Helens and Wigan were apt, he said, to scoff at its attractions, hut he pro tested against the idea that the county had no rustic charms out of which associations not easily forgotten might arise. His early life was spent in that part of the county which extends from Liverpool to Preston and Southport —that flat country which those who did not understand the true charm of country life or the true beauty of landscape sometimes describ3d as uninteresting—and it was there he first learnt to love the country. " Whenever I hear the Lancashire accent," said Sir Joseph, "it seems to bring to me an assurance —it may be somewhat blunt and not very reverential —of the most thorough and genuine kindness."

* * * Ultra-Imperialists of the Conservative type like Alderman Bennett ought to take special note of ,the fact that on Monday the " Times " admitted in the handsomest way that time has vindicated the wisdom of Liberal policy in South Africa. It said : Although in our opinion at the time the Govern- ment incurred considerable risks by immediate bestowal of self-government upon the Transvaal and the Orange River C)lony, we frankly admit that the experiment has been justified by the event. Smith Africa happily is not a subject of Imperial anxiety. As the result of Liberal plicy —hotly opposed and strongly condemned by (for instance) Mr. Balfour and Lord tfilner—South Africa has now ceased to be what it certainly has been, a "subject of Imperial anxiety." Amid all the froth about Empire here is one very solid achievement -to the credit of the Liberal party. Our friends on the other side will do well to remember it when next they are inclined to attack the Liberal rarty for its lack of Imperialism.

* * Purists periodically agitate for the suppression of reports of the evidence in divoice cases, but we imagine the" reform" has few supporters amid the rank and file of the great army of newspaper readers. There are strong moral arguments, too.-in favour of continuing the present practice. Ant one fact is incontestable and this is that People like to know all about their neighbours' marital misdnings. The information which even the carefully edited newspaper provides of a cause celebre ia usually interesting beyond the ordinary.. Putting the Sterling case on one side, take the snit that a Japanese lady is bringing against her Japanese husband in Washington. The charges she brings against him are that he has failed to enter- tain her with witty conversation, that he has become bald, that he has developed a habit of cracking his knuckles, and that he has grown warts. The stages by which a lack of marital integrity has drawn him down to these depths of abandoned villainy should certainly be disclosed, in the public interest; and who can deny that the details are interesting? And how are people to find the answer to the query: "Is marriage a failure ? " unless they cm learn something from the experience of others.

Surely one of the saddest stories of "drunken children " was that told at the Liverpool Licensing Sessions last week. A little girl of ten—mark the age—had stolen some clothing, which she got another girl ta.pawn. With the proc,eeds she went with others to a public-house, and asked for drink, which was refused. She then invited an older girl, who could be legitimately served, to purchase some whisky at the same house. Later, with the assistance of a drunken person at the bar, who received a halfpenny RR a reward, she bought a sixpenny bottle of port. Two of the children consumed it in an entry, and were taken to the hospital ill: One of them, on being asked to give her version of the, story, said that one of the others, being asked if the wine would make her drunk, told her: "If it does, put your head under the cold-water tap as mother does, and that will make you sober again." "As mother does ! " There is just one bright feature in this case. One of the five little girls did not taste of the wine, or the whisky, because she was a teetotaler, possibly a member of a band of hope. The desirability of juvenile abstinence from both alcohol and tobacco is so palpable that it needed only this revolting case to ensure redoubled attention to scientific instruction on the subject in the elementary schools.

THE LAW AS TO DISQUALIFICATION. The law as to disqualification is that when a candidate is unseated as a result of his own corrupt practices at a Municipal Election he is debarred from ever again entering the Town Council or holding a corporate office. If he is found guilty by his agents of a corrupt practice, he is not capable of being elected to or holding any corporate office for three years.

Beetherton, G.Pilling, S.Horton, E. Horton, G. Wilson, R. Nixon, J. Renshaw, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), T. Cook,J. Pearson W. R. de Prez (relieving officers), and T. Mr. Spruce stated that Mr. Baysa was an efficient officer and the House Cammittee had decided to ask him to accept an addition ot Zi to his salary, making it £35. After a lengthy conversation Nlr. Sayse agreed to accept the proposition and continue an employee at the Workhouse. .

Mr. Clifford Muspratt leotured, at the Liberal Club, Widnes, on Tuesday night, on "The Reform Bills and the Future of the. Franchise." Alderman Sam Quinn presided. The lecturer dealt first with the historical side of his subject, and went on to say that he thought the first measure of progress should be on the lines introduced by the Liberal Government three years ago, and the paramount feature of which was the abolition of plural voting. Without this it was impossible to gauge the real and relative 1 size of a constituency. It had been said that the bill had been brought forward for party gain. The argument against this was that it was opposed for fear of party loss. A fair measure of redistribu6ion would be impossible until plural voting was done away with. The lecturer dealt with anomalies of the fran- chise. He urged that the qualifying period should be lessened. At present it often occurred that a man bad .1 to wait two and a half years before getting on the register. Men should also be able to transfer their votes more easily when they moved. There was the rock upon which they all split—women's suffrage. His personal views were entirely in favour of women's suffrage. He disapproved of physical force and of the suffragettes, but he would never swerve from his allegi- ance to women's suffrage. If the Liberal Government ' did not give the women the vote, sooner or later the Tories would follow out their old policy of " dishing the Whigs," and pass a measure for female suffrage. In concluding, the lecturer dealt with the question of adult suffrage and proportional representation, warmly . supporting both proposals. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. _ John Quigley, aged four years, of Gladstone-street, died in the Providence Hospital, St, Helens, early on Monday morning from bnrns. The child was admitted to the hospital on Sunday afternoon, having been attended by Dr. Wilson, but it was evident from the first that the case was hopeless.. ST. TIELENS SOCIALISTS. Mr. J. Parker, M.P. (Halifax), addressing the St. Helens Socialists on Monday afternoon, said the poverty problem still challenged the reason and conscience of man, and instead of becoming less acute as national wealth increased it actually became more serious day by day. There were more people hitt state of abject poverty in England to-day than there were six centuries ago. It was the business of the Labour party to put to the front, and keep to the front, the provision of the right to work for every citizen. though he did not believe it was possible to solve the unemployed pro- blem short of Socialism. Sr. HELENS PARKS AND FOOTBALLERS.

! At the meeting of the St. Helens Parks Committee on Wednesday, Mr. 11. H. Peet presiding, letters from the St. Helens Association League, the Sunday School League, and the School Sports' Committee were reported to have been received asking for permission to play football matches in the parks. The committee recently gave permission to the Junior Rugby League, but as soon as this became known letters poured in from all sides asking for similar treatment. Ihe Mayor (Mr. Foote) said that the parks and recreation grounds ought to be reserved for the childrett. They could not flad room for all these football clubs, and that view was adopted, the committee decining to refuse all applica- tions but that of the School Sports' Committee for practice games. Afterwards the committee appointed Mr. Smetham, of Taylor Park, as head gardener ar,d superintendent of the parks. FOUR MONTHS FOR THEFT. Elizabeth Speaktban, married woman, of Gorsey- brow, Billinge, was charged at St. Helens on Monday, with two eases of theft. The evidence was that on Saturday morning the woman went to Mr. kloxon's pawnshop ia Claugtdon-street to redeem two pledges. Afterwards a table cover was missed, and the police were informed. They went in search of the woman, Detective Roe found her in Back College-street. She had a parcel which contained the table cover, and the woman was locked up. The detective, with Inspector Dunn, then went to the woman's house at Billinge. About twenty pawntickets were found in the hause • behind a picture. One of these tickets teferred to a I dress which had been stolen from the same place on • September 15. Mrs. Speakman admitted the thefts. The woman was before the court in November last for being drunk in charge of a child,and she served fourteen days in gaol. The Bishop of Liverpool, having consulted with the Vicar of Haydock, Her. Ireland, and the legal repre- sentatives of the ecclesiastical authorities, has made certain proposals with a view to settling the difficulty that has arisen in connection with the patronage of the new parish of St. Mark's, litydock. Tee terms of the proposed arrangement were placed before the Council of St. Mark's on Monday night by the Rev. T. S. Storey, curate-in-charge, but the meeting declined to Accept them. •

div.head: EARLESTOWN'S NEW CHIEF OF POLICE.
div.p: EARLESTOWN'S NEW CHIEF OF POLICE.

Tue new Police inspector at Earlestowa is Inspector Carr, late of Stretford, Alanchester, who has a long record of service in Lancashire. Baginning as a cont stable in Stretford, he was afterwards 4tationed at Milurow and Clitheroe, was made acting sergeaat at Great Harwood, with recognition of special merit, and sergeant at Wualley. Going further north; he was eighteen months at Dalton-iu-Furness, and was maved thence to Askam, and after a time back to St.retford, where he has been stationed for the last six years, with high commendation for his services, and on January 22nd was chosen as Inspector for Earlestown.• He has just taken up his residence here. BOYS IN THE DAIRY.

At Newten Petty Sessions last Tnuraday,MOPS Vincent Jackson and Frank Jackson were charged with breaking and-entering the lock-up shop of the Maypole Dairy Co. in Market-street, EAriestown, on the 4th inst., and on another oceasion between January 21 and 23, and with damaging butter, etc., to the extent of £l. —frank Jackson was dissharged, being only six years of age. The other bay, aged 11, admitted the offence. —Mr. 'Jackson, manager for the Maypole Dairy Co., said he found damage done on the premises, and he and P.C.'s Wnittle and Lonnie watched. It happened four times altogether, and on the afternoon of Thursday, the 4th inst., they caught-the little boo at the back 'trying to get in. The damage done was to butter, margarine, and gas mantles. His firm did not want to press the case hardly against the boy.—The boy's mother was in Court, and said he was very mischievous. He had been punished every way at home.—lnspector Morgan said the police had reports of his pilfering habits.—Tne Bench ordered the boy to have three strokes with a birch a rod, and added that there was blame a..taching to the Sinn for not making the premises more secure.

div.head: EAALESTOWN MAN'S CONIPENSATION.
div.p: EAALESTOWN MAN'S CONIPENSATION.

At the Warriugtou County—CO-li-rOn--1.;;;;;d-st;,- "before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, K.U., F. A. Murphy, Auto Bright Hexagon Nut Works, Honduras- Street, Oldham, brought an applicatiOn for the review of an award under tile Workmen's Compensation Act made to Andrew Concannon, Cross-lane, liierlestown. Mr. Merriman, barrister (instructed by Air. Alfred Pearsor, Manchester) made the application, and Mr. B. A. Connor, of Warrington, appeared for Concannon.—lt appeared that Cencanuon met with an accident wkilst following his employment on October 21st, 1905, and lost three fingers of his left hand. On November Ist, 1906, application was made for the registration of en agreement for the payment of full compensation- 14s. 2d. par week—and Murphy asked for a reduction of the amount. His Honour declined to make any reduc- tion but expressed the strong view that the man ought to make strenuous efforts to get work and if be did not,an application for review in a short perion would receive favourable consideration. Cmcannon had not worked with the firm since, *tad they knew nothing about him until the present application was filed. Oa February 16th they received a letter from his solicitor stating that Coucannon's average weekly earnings during the past year had been 17s. Oil, and in view of that he was willing to agree to a diminution of the compensation by 3s. 4d. a week. Mr. Merriman cobtended that offer was not a fair one. Cancannon's weekly wages before the accident were 235. 4d., and he stated that he now received 17s. Gd., sb that the loss was 10s. 10d. In addition, however, he bad the 14s. 2d. compensation, so that he had really been receiving 31s. Bd. as against the 28s. 4d. before the accident. If a deduction of only 3s. 4d. were made, it would mean that the firm would be bearing thp whole of the loss between his estimated earnings at present and his wages before the accideut.—Dr. Riche °rid stated that had examined tioncaunon and saw no reason why he should not follow any occupation that did not involve a firm grip with the left hand.—Mr. Connor submitted that Concannon would never be able to follow his former occupation and he had great difficulty in getting any work at all. At present be was trying to gain a livelihood by means of an insurance book.— Concaunon was called and gave evidence as to his inability to obtain employmtmt at local works.—James Anderton, a works foreman, stated that in his opinion Cancannon could not possibly work the machine at which he was engaged before the accident —His Honour decided to reduce the award ff om 145.2 d. to ss. 51. per week, each pirty to pay their own costs

Every Picture us a Story.'
other tells how size Lost her First Two Babies through Dropsy and Kidney Complaint before her Cure by Doan's Backache Kidney Pills. She is now the proud mother of a bonny little girl.

Mrs. Sanders, 3. Stanway Cottages, F.astworth- Toad, Chertsey, Surrey, says :—"At the time I was looking forward to my first baby—in 1906 was scarcely ever well. My heart pained dreadfully, and 1 -suffered with pains in the side and loins. Sometimes after I hthd been seated a little while I -could scarcely manage to get up from the chair, my joints were so stiff and rheumatic. " How tc drag myself about the house T hardly knew. Often I would come over quite giddy. My eves were dark and puffy, and ray legs swelled with water to a great size (dropsy). "My husband and I were alarmed at this break- down in my health, and our worst fears were realised, when, in December (1906), my baby was born flee weeks prematurely. He lived only eight days. "To our dismay. the same distressing symptoms of dropsy and kidney complaint appeared the following summer, when, for the second time, I was expecting to become a mother, and the terrible experience of 1906 was repeated—my second baby was a month prematurely born. She lived but five weeks. "I grew as downcast and dejected as only a woman can be when her greatesthopes are shattered, for I began to fear I should never be able to rear ti child. Happily, however, just at this time one of my relatives sent me a newspaper cutting about Mrs. Sarson, of Great Dalby, Melton Mowbray' who had lost her first three babies through kidney disorders and dropsy before her cure by Doan's Backache Kidney Pills, and afterwards became

"To my great joy the medicine kept me entirely free from the dropsy and kidney com- plaint. I went my full time and baby was born healthy and bonny. div.head: .ROYAL COURT THEATRE
div.p: .ROYAL COURT THEATRE
The Pantomime, " Dick Whittington."

The concluding performances of Mr. Elwin C. Jazou's pantomime" Dick Whittington" will be given this afternoon and evening. Good houses have ben the rule throughout the week, and the bright scenes, pretty dresses, and smart dancing have won hearty appreciation. The personnel of this psntotnime is also very good, Miss Maud Beaumont heading a very capable company as principal boy in the part of Jack. She throws any amount of dash into her acting, and earns hearty applause for her songs. Miss Vera Snowdon is a very attractive Alice, and the fun is fast and furious when Mr. Fred Ward as Jack, the idle apprentice, is on the stage. The cat plays an important part in the story as well as in the panto- mime, and Willie Vanda makes an excellent "Thomas." A number of special turns are introduced, and the whole show is full of variety and attractiveness.
NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. THE VILLAGE BLACKSMITH.

This great. play is such a strong local favourite that it is unnecessary to write at any length of it in view of its presentation at the Royal Court Theatre, for six nights next week. Many readers are aware that it' ptesents some highly sensational situations, including an exciting wrestling encounter, and affords plenty of opportunity for the display of dramatic talent. We have in the title role that clever actor, Mr. Sam Livesey, who will assuredly look the part, as he is a man of brawny muscles and fine presence. The cast includes Messrs. Albert Sinclair Fred !laming, Edwin Maydew, Thomas E. Marshall, Gus Ratcliffe, A. Walker, G. Wilton, B. Morris, E. Butler, S. Ball, Misses T. C. Livesey, Edith Giddens, Cassie le Grand, Kathleeh Saunders, and that clever actress, Miss Mani° Edwards.

div.head: DUST PROBLA
div.p: THE DUST PROBLA

The dust problem in connection with motor- cars, is again said-to have been settled in more senses than one. The County Etngineering Company, of Thornton Heath, have devised a funnel-shaped receptacle at the back of each wheel at the point where the dust would be otherwise dispersed, and the force of the air pressure on the vacuum caused by the wheel's motion will force the rising dust backwards, and the funnel will catch it. When two pounds' ,weight has been thus collected it will be auto- matically damped by water set free from a tank by its own weight and then dropped on the road. The arrangement will dispose of 90 per cent, of the dust which would be otherwise thrown up in clouds.

Umbrellas.—A small amount of forethought on our part will make our umbrellas last twice as long as if they were paid no regard to. First of all, when you come in with a wet umbrella, open it out in an empty room to dry; never put it away in an umbrella-stand while damp. And if you are not using it, put it away loosely rolled up. If it is tightly rolled, it is apt to cut the silk.

1117 DEAR CHILDREN, Many thanks for the nice letters received during the past week. You will remember that. I asked you specially not to forget to send in either letters or contribution ; well, to judge by my post-bag, my appeal has not gone unheeded. lam glad of this, as letters from my members are very pleasing to me. I have been very interested in the essays received on "How to make people happy." My young friends seem to have many ideas on this subject, although I must say that many to hand are exceedingly good. It's a very easy subject, so I hope to receive a lot more.
Whenever you have a few minutes to spare sit down and write me a letter telling me about your home life, and your pets and garden.
Well, I will leave you to think this over. With love, UNCLE NED.
MEG, THE MATCH-GIRL. (Continued from last week.)

"But why am I here?" asked Meg feebly. "'When the horse kicked you," she began, "the driver managed to pull it up, and when they examined you they found that you had a wound in your head, and that you were unconscious. A docter arrived upon the scene, and he said that you would require careful nursing, so as no one knew you, or where you lived, I brought you home, but that is two days ago, and your relatives will be uneasy, so if you will tell me your name and where you live, I will let them know," she concluded, stroking .Me'ws curly hair. "My name is Meg Brown, but I have no home."

"No home, poor child. Have you no parents ? " asked the lady gently. "No, my father died five years ago, and my mother nearly a month since," she answered, bursting into tears. "There, there, do not cry," whispered the lady stooping and kissing her.

"Dear lady, what is your name?" asked Meg shyly. "Mrs. Dennis," she said, with a smile. "But Madge is waiting to thank you. Madge, Madge," she called. Madge came in and the baby toddled in after her. She came to the bed- side, and said in a lisping tone: " I thank you very much for saving my life. Papa says it was very brave of you,"—she paused as though at a loss what else to say, and looked straight up into Meg's face—" I have forgotten all mother told me to say, but please may I kiss you?" Meg bent her head and both Madge and Eric kissed her. Then Mr. Dennis came in, and he was such a nice kind man, that Meg forgot her shyness, and told them all about herself, and how she had lived since mother died. Then both Mr. and Mrs. Dennis said that she would have to stay and live with them, and so " Meg the Match-girl," found a home at last. MAY BLOSSOM.
lIOW TO MAKE OTHERS HAPPY.

First, be happy yourself. Contentment brings happiness. Think how much other people's temper is sweetened through you being happy. For example, if children are discon- tented the parents arc unhappy, while a bright, happy child is 'worth its weight in gold to the home. Practise daily to carry a smile on your face—you never know what that smile does. When you (yourself) are happy, think what you can do to improve others. It May be there is a hospital near the home, think what you. might do for the sick. A bunch of flowers taken there may be the means of making many happy. There are always poor children waiting for your kindness; they are always wanting some article of dress. By saving odd coppers you could supply them with this. Sometimes in the city an old woman would like to be guided across the street—just help her, and then she will be happy. Just think of what you can do, and many things will rise up in your mind. Much co abe done to complete the happiness of others. a little child falls down, pick it up, not let it lay deserted and hurt. If your friend is carrying two baskets, and you have nothing in your hands, take one. Even little acts like this is being kind. Once a poor little girl Itly ill; she wanted to do something for her less fortunate brothers and sisters. She was too weak to sew or knit. What could she do? A factory in which many women and girls worked was situated not far from the house, and many had to pass to get to it. The girl's couch was placed near the window. "She would smile to all who passed." This she did, and many going to work misrable, sulky, and hungry, turned their eyes to the window, and saw the smiling face. They were made happy, only by her smile. Quite a heap of sympathising letters came to the invalided girl, and most told her how happy her smile had made them.
"Little deeds of kindness, Little words of love, Make our earth an Eden, Like the heaven above." • FLORENCE ELLEN DARK.

div.head: BURSAR SYSTEW.
div.p: THE BURSAR SYSTEW.

The Rev. Canon STEVENSON, in moving the confirma- tion of the minutes of the School Ntanageraent Com- mittee, alluded to the following minute :—" A report by the Director of E location on the suggested sub- stitution of the bursar for the pupil-te 'cher system, ' having been considered, it was resolved (a) that, on and after the Ist August, 1909, the bursar and student- , teacher system be substituted for the pupil-teacher system in the borough ; and (b) that the salaries to be paid to student-teachers be at the rate of .£2O per : annum in the case of girls, awl £23 per annum in the case of boys. (a) That the Blard of Education he approached with a view to provision being made in their future regulations dealing with this matter for the candidates for bursarships to be required to spend some little time teaching in chosen public elementary schools for the pttrpose of showing their probable suitability or otherwise for the teaching profession ; and (b) that the matter be brought to the notice of the Association of Education Committees with a view to securing the support of that body to this action." Canon Stevenson said that the time had come to adopt the bursar system, and if they did not, do so they would place their young people at a dis- advantage compared to those living in other towns. At present, however, the system had a serious blot. These boys and girls were choosing to become busars, which meant the teachers of the future, without any attempt being made to find out whether they had the necessary ability for that particular profession. There- fore the committee, had decided to make some repre- sentation to the Board of Eincation, and to the Association of Education Committees which dealt with the matter in the hope that they would be able to place the children for a short time in a school with a view to ascertaininz whether they were likely (to use the Lancashire phrase) to " shape." (Hear, hear, and laughter.)
Mr. UPSON seconded the confirmation of the minutes and it was agreed to.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. The Rev. T. R. Matthews appeared in the chair after a long absence through illness, and there were also present : -Mrs. Simpson, Miss Broadbent, Dr. Murray, Messrs. G. Mather, A. J. Jolley, W. Furness, NV. C. Brooks, \V. Houghton, W. Plannagau, P. Longtori, A. Brooks, R. Forshaw, A. Bottomley (clerk), R. W. Peacock (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of the Cottage Homes).

THE CHAIRMAN.S RETURN. Mr. M.YrttEtt said he would only be echoing the sentiments of all present when he said how pleased they ware to see the Chairman back amongst them, restored to health and strength, and their hope Was that he might long be spared. The CHAIRMAN said he was thank fnl to say he had returned very much refreshed—but not with new wine. (Laughter).

The whole matter arose from the question of ahether Dr. Hodgkinson should be put in telephonic communication with the Workhouse or not and the special committee came to the above conclusion by a majority, lie would have preferred, instead of the others being taken off the telephone,that Dr. Ilodgkinson should have been placed on. A TRUE STORY OF A DAKOTA BLIZZARD. (Continued from last week.)

So, though Alice and Molly sobbed in concert, she heaped fresh coal on the fire, wrapped herself in her warmest clothing, drawing on high fur I:ned rubber boots, put a flask of brandy in her pocket, and took the compass from the mantel-shelf to show her the way ; for not even a shadow of the barn (although it was larger than the house) was visible through the storm. Then, taking the clothes- line, she tied one end of the rope tightly around her waist, and, making the othtt last to the knob of the outer door, set out. Upon her perilous journey of twenty yards dile north, where she knew the barn must be. Again and again she . was beaten down to the ground by the violence of the wind ; but she struggled on, keeping the direction of the needle of the compass, and at last reached the side of the barn. Thence she carefully felt her way— fortunately taking the right course—and, finding the door, beat on it with all her might. It was opened by her brothers, and, in the same breath, all, asked the same question, she ol them, and they of her :
" Where is father?" "I don't know. I came to see!" and "He started for the house half an hour ago, telling us to stay here. until he cam 2. back," %%ere simultaneous answevs.
'Didn't he take a rope ? " asked Dora, eagerly.
." Of course he did. It is tied outside some- where," said the oldest boy, a year or two her senior,

" Then we must follow it and find him. Alice begged me not to come, but I felt sure something was wrong. Come, Joe, we mustn't lose a minute. Harry and Jack must stay here. Do you hear, boys ? " The younger lads begged to come too, but Dora and Joe did not stay to listen. "We mustn't risk their lives, too," she said, huskily. They found the rope covered with sn )w, and to their surprise stretched taut. "He must have got to the house safe," said Joe, joyfully.

_ But Dora shook her head. "No, it doesn't point south, as it would ,f he were at home. Besides, 1 shouted all the time as I came along, and we couldn't have passed each other. He has gone the wrong way." Meanwhile, clinging to each other, they were folloMng the rope, which slanted lower and lower until, a few feet away, they found it wrapped around the root of a small tree. It was harder to keep hold of it now, but Joe had brought a snow-staff with a sharp hook at °tr.i end, and with this it was possible to follow the rope's cours Tlpy shouted again and again, at the top- of their clear, young voices. There was no answer. Still they toiled on, amid it was not long (though it seemed an ont'e) before they stumbled over a snow-covered heap. It was the body of their father .lying where, exhausted by cold and fatigue, he had fallen helplessly to the ground. Raising his head, pora poured part of the contents of the flask down his tlyroat. He moaned faintly. He was alive I They lifted him, and dragged him along, vainly trying to make him walk, since exercise was the best means of saving his life. # Guided by Dora's rope, which she had wound up after a fashion, thanks to her thick fur gloves, they at last reached the warm kitchen, where a vigorous course of rubbing with snow soon restored their fa her to perfect consciousnesm, and brought him out of danger. He had lost his way, and in his bewilder- ment had gone around the tree, unconsciously crossing his rope. Thence he had gone to the end of his tether, and in trying to get back to the barn, had found the rope frozen fast to the ground. In his efforts ,to •free U, he had been blown down, and thus dropped the end which he held—for he had not taken Dora's w:se precaution of tying it around the body. H. 4 was unable to find it with Ifs numb fingers. Ile shouted Vainly for aid, and, afra:d to move in any direction,. wisely remained where he was. He tried hard to keep in motion, but was overcome by cold, and beaten down by the force of the storm. He must inevitably have been frozen to death but for Dora's hero:c search for him. And the boys in the barn? Oh, Joe went back for them as soon as their father was safe, and they all ate dinner together, but some three hours later than usual.

A most amusing incident occurred recently at a London Club. One night after Mr. Bertram, the conjurer, had exhibited some tricks with cards, a rather noisy member observed, " What nonsense ! It's all sleight of hand, and I'll play you for all you're worth at ecarte, despite your nimble finger- ing." • Quick as lightning the necromancer said, "Sir, I could not afford to accept your challenge.. See, you have the four kings con- cealed up your left sleeve!" and lie drew the cards from the challenger's coat.

It was his first visit to the City. As he stood on the curbstone shaking his side with laughter, he was abcosted by: "What's the fun, stranger?" " Fun! Can't you see it? Just look how that thing (pointing to a watering-cart) leaks! Why, the fool won't have a drop left when he gets home." —4--

It has been discovered, says the Universily Corr e.s. pondent, that radium rays act as a stimulus to the growth of plants. Up to a certain point, exposure to the rays results in considerably - increased growth of germinat- ing seeds, but if the strength or duration of the treatment is increased beyond this point there ensues a falling off, ending in complete stoppage of growth.

div.head: POST-CARDS.
div.p: POST-CARDS.

The prepaid rate -oi-p-os-t;i:E;;;11 every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 51 inches in length by 31 inckes in width, or be less than 3t inches in length by 21 inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and finch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter.

HALFPENNY PACKET POST. The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only fDr packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, itc., not. in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST.

The prepaid rale-Of-PO-stage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other printed matter.

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: For a parcel ... ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 exceeding 1 lb. ff 2 lb. 0 4 „ 2 lb. ff 3 lb. 0 5 ft „ 3 lb. f t 5 lb. 0 6 „ 5 lb. ft 7 lb. 0 7 , f tv 7 lb. 27 8 lb. 0 8 ” ~ 8 lb. f , 9 lb. 0 9 f, 9 lb. tf 10 lb. 0 10 • /P f, 10 lb. " 11 lb. 011 No parcel may exceed 11 lb. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel is:— Greatest len.th 3 ft. 6 in. Greatest length and girth combined _ 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring Mt. 6in. in its longest dimensions a 4 much as 21t. 6in. round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker; thus, if it measure no more than Mt. in length, it may measure as much as 3ft. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel "Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving.

div.head: PARCELS -(FOREIGN AND COLONIAL).
div.p: PARCELS -(FOREIGN AND COLONIAL).

Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a Id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding El, 2d.; .C 3 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 6d.; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order i may be issued for places abroad varies n each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, 6d. ; cud above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 6d. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. OSTAL ORDERS. These are obtat ble at any money order.office in the United Kingd m, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by 6d., from 6d. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are :—ld. up to 2s. 6d.; Id. up to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums. TELEGRAMS (INLAND). - - - . . .

The Postmaster-General possesses,atmost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,colleciAng and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d. which covers Li words, and an additional id. For each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far-as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handtd to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is Li is.

div.head: TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL)
div.p: TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL)
Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here.

div.head: POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.

These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaclaes that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is or over: a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 21 per cent. Any amount up to and including £1 may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller,of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can bee xpedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegra ms.

div.head: MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REQULATIONS.
div.p: MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REQULATIONS.

Each one must be registered with the council of a county orcounty borough, the fee being £1 fored motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. A register a number isassigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep affixed when driving. Each driver must possess a license, costing 55., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other nffences. The highest speetttat which a car may be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions.
It is an offence under the Motor Car Act (1903), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case.

In the event of an accident to any person due to the presence of the motor car on the road, the driver must supply his name and address, and the owner and number of the oar under heavy penalties. The driver must pro- duce his licence at the request of a constable. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK LINE CHARGES. _

div.head: DRILLING HOLES IN GLASS.
div.p: DRILLING HOLES IN GLASS.

Ms,ny people think that it is a very hard j..-)b to drill holes in glass, but this is not so. It requires, of course, more time and more care than drilling in metal, because there is greater danger of breaking the glass. The drill is made of a stecl rod or an old three- cornered file. One of its ends is ground to a long tapering triangle-shaped point. It is placed in a swiftly-revolving chuck (lathe or electric hand - drilling machine), and the glass pressed against it very gently. The work should be held in the hands in order to feel the pressure against the drill. As a lubricaut turpentine is used. ,

div.head: LIQUID HELIUM.
div.p: LIQUID HELIUM.

In some experiments with the liquefaction of helium, Professor Onnes performed a labour of the 'mist exhausting description. " Not only," we are told, " was the whole ap- paratus, with its subsidiary arrangements, tested to its utmost capacity, but the physical energies of the Professor and his assistants were well-nigh exhausted by the prolonged struggle." This, comments an American magazine, is likely to give to most readers an entirely novel idea of the .labours of the labo- ratory. When the absolute zero is approached the obstacles that have to be overcome in order to lower the temperature. a, few degrees are immense. The boiling-point of liquid helium is 4ideg. Cent. above absolute. zero. By great effort the temperature was reduced to 3deg. Cent., but without affecting the mo- bility of the liquid.

div.head: ELECTRIC WELDING.
div.p: ELECTRIC WELDING.

Mr. L. S. Lachman has devised a new process of electric welding which makes it possible, says the Scientific American, to employ steel instead of malleable iron in the manufacture of numerous articles. As two pieces of metal of unequal sections cannot be welded together satisfactorily Lachman has one piece cast with a projecting edge and the other with a point. The two projections, _forced together by a hydraulic press, are included.in an elec-

tric circuit, of which they form the segment of highest resistance. Hence, when a strong current is caused ,to flow through them, they are heated nearly or quite to the melting point and, being subjected to great pressure, quickly become welded together, and attach themselves to each other more firmly than they could be attached by means of rivets, be- cause there is no break in the continuity of the metal.
PROTECTION OF RIVER BANKS

The statement is constantly met that forests are very efficacious in the protection of river banks from underyining and steep slopes from sliding. The exact rverse is the case, says the Engineer. As &Wry river engineer knows, nothing is more disastrous to a river bank on an alluvial stream than heavy trees. This is due partly to the great weight, but in large part to the swaying effect of the wind and the enormous leverage of the long trunks, which pry up the ground and facilitate the tendency to undermining. One of the regular policies of river control is to cut down these trees for a distance back from the edge of the bank wherever complications with private ownership do not prevent. Snags and drift- wood in the channels have always been amongst the most serious obstacles to naviga- tion on streams flowing between forest- covered banks. Likewise where railway or highway grading cuts the skin of unstable mountain slopes, the presence of large trees immediately above tends- powerfully to loosen the ground and cause it to slide, and in such cases it is necessary to cut down the timber.

div.head: CURIOUS ALTERATION OF TIN.
div.p: CURIOUS ALTERATION OF TIN.

A phenomenon presenting several *points of resemblance to bacterial infection, but ap- parently of an inorganic nature, has been de- scribed by Dr. von Hasslinger. A piece of tin plate that had been kept for about two years at a temperature of 16deg. to 45deg. Centi- grade Wat 3 found to have completely changed its appearance, the surface having become granular and dull. When partieles from the surface of this grey tin were brought into con- tact with other pieces of tin a sort Of inocula- tion occurred, and the bright surfaces soon became covered with dull patches, which de- veloped at the rate of several millimetres a day. The growth of this so-called "tin pest was not affected by a rise in temperature, and in this respect it differed from bacterial growth on organic substances; but the de- velopment of the patches was less vigorous at a distance . from, the point of inoculation. Tin that had undergone this alteration melted at a lower temperature (205 deg. C.) than the original tin, which melted at 231-232 deg. C. On melting the grey tin it regained its •nor- mal characteristics and again melted at the original temperature. No explanation, says Knowledge, has yet been suggested for this curious alteration, wljich appears, however, to be due to.the formation cf an allotropic modification of tin.

div.head: WORM AND SEAWEED,
div.p: WORM AND SEAWEED,

Certain yellow-brown cells vt hich are pre- sent in a 3pecies of marine worms (Convouita paradoxa) seem to mark a case of what biolo- gists call symbieGis—a living together of two organisms or mutual advantage. In this case we have a seaweed living in a worm. For, according to the investigations of Mr. F. Keeble, published in. the Quarterly Jour- nal of Microscopical Science, the yellow- brown cells found in the worms are a species of alga. They are not found in the eggs or newly-hatched worms, and if these are kept in filtered sea-water they are not developed. If, however, they are brought into contact with seaweed from the zone inhabited by the worms, they become infected. What, then, are tho

div.head: BENEFITS TO WORM AND SEAWEED
div.p: BENEFITS TO WORM AND SEAWEED

from this strange partnership? The worm fceds on the algal cells. These latter secrete fat globules, which serve as food reserves for the worm. A worm cannot properly develop without them. If starved they digest their algal cells till nothing remains of them. Thus the worm may be said .to grow its vegetables in its (mu tissues. There is perhaps the addi- tional advantage that the worm thus gets rid of its waste nitrogenous products, for it is on these that the alga feeds.- The benefit to the latter' is a convenient place of growth, and an abundant supply of nitrogenous matters

div.head: AN IMPROVED MAGNETOMETER
div.p: AN IMPROVED MAGNETOMETER

Messrs. J. G. Grcy and A. D. Ross, of Glasgow University, have. designed a new type of magnetometer. They point out that in the usual type Qf magnetometer thi testing of feebly magnetic substances in high fields was a matter of extreme difficulty owing to the great accuracy required in compensating the effects of the electric current passing through the system. Moreover, a slight, and indeed almost unirvoidable, error in the alignment of the coils may produce errors amounting to several per cent. In the new type of instru- ment the usual single compensating Oil ,is re- . placed by thkee coils, viz., an ordinary com- pensator for approximate • aclkistment, a second but distant coil for fine adjustment, and a third coil pled due north or south of the magnetometer needle which removes all error due to want of proper alignment of the other coils. The whole system is rigidly mounted on a strong bed-plate, and clamping arrangements are provided whereby the mov- ing parts can be accurately fixed where de- sired. The Gray-Ross • instrument • with its acdessories possesses the following advant- ages: (1) Suitable alike for strongly or feebly magnetic substances; (2) capable of perfect and rapid adjustment; (3) available for mag- netising fields up to 400 c.a.s. units; (4) tests Jan be made at all temperatures from that of Liquid hydrogen to I,2oodeg. Centigrade; (5) I it is specially adapted for investigations ot tho effective lengths of magnets:,
The Examiner, Saturday February 20, '1909.

div.head: Warrington's Second Fixture with the Kangaroos.
div.p: Warrington's Second Fixture with the Kangaroos.

Warrington were the first team to have a second fixture with the kangaroos, and the match took place at Wilderspool on Saturday in beautiful weather. Popular prices were charged and there was a crowd of over 7,000, the gate money totalling £l5O, of which the tourists received 60 per cent. Warrington had their strongest team in the field, and the Australians were also well represented, though three prominent backs in Devereaux, Deane, and Bolewski stood down owing to injury. Warrington's recent fine form suggested that they would record a second victory over the Colonials, but. the latter played a great game and succeeded in drawing the match. Teams and officials' : Warrington—LiHey, back ; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Treharne, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Jenkins, half backs; Neill, Dom ell, Thomas, A. E. Boardman Belton, and Shugars, forwards. Australians—Hedley, back ; Messenger, Frawley, Heidke, and Anderson, three-quarter becks ; Butler and Holloway, half backs ; Gums, McCabe, O'Malley, Walsh, Hennessey, and Cann, forwards. , Referee, Mr. H. Farrar, Keighley. Touch judges, Messrs. J. Houghton and Sergt.-Major Hannaford, St. Helens.

Messenger started the game and the Australians were soon on the attack. Tilley and Dickenson being severely tested. A run by Brooks and Dickenson took play past the centre, but the Tisitors returned to the attack with dashing forward play, O'Malley leading the rush in fine style. Smart play by Fish on the lett again drove the Australians out, but from near centre Messenger placed a fine goal. Brooks got away soon after the, re-start, but tiara was absence of finish, and Messenger was to the fore in forcing matters at the Warrington end. The Colonial came near dropping a goal, and Fish retaliating, Thomas was held up inches short of the lice. The pressure was maintained, and from a pack near the line Holloway lost the ball and Jenkins crossed, but Fish missed the goal shot. Brooks had a kick charged,and O'Malley took the ball over,but failed to get up in time to complete the try. Australia had their reward near the interval, for Messenger put on the finishing touch to passing between Anderson and Heidke and at the interval the Colonials led by 1 goal and 1 try (5 points), to Warrington 1 try (3 points). Warrington re-opened in vigorous style and brilliant work by Fish and Dickenson carried play well into the Australian quarter. Taylor run well and took play to the line where a series of tough scrummages were fought out before Messenger got hold and relieve i with a huge kick to centre. Warrington tried hard to get the lead and there was a groan of disappointment when, after fine work by the home left wing, Dickenson raced behind the posts and was recalled by the whistle for a forward pass. The decision was a doubtful one, and it xi ad some consolation when Thomas took a penalty kick and equalised the scores. Some vigorous play by the Australians caused Tilley to get in difficulties but the defence prevailed. in the last stages Warrington pressed bard. Neill passed well at a critical moment. ,ind Fish completed a try after a grand run. Warring- ton still attacked, but being loose in their vrok Messenger intervened, and racing away handed on to Frawley, who got in at the corny. Messenger had the issue of the game in his hands when be kicked at goal, but though well directed the ball patsed a yard outside the posts. Er suit :—Warrington l goal and 2 tries (8 points), Australia, 1 goal and 2 tries (8 points).

div.head: WIDNES v. BATLEY.
div.p: WIDNES v. BATLEY.

Played at Widnes, b72,10r-e. i3OOT-fieCtators. Widnes got into their (pponents' "25," Lut Will Davies relieved with a gocd run. When te play was at centre Moran mulled badly, and Will Davies gathered finely and raced over the line. The same player placed a goal Half-time :—Batley, 1 goal and 1 try (5 points),Widnes nil.

The second half opened in favour of Widnts, and from several scrummages on the line the home backs made desperate attempts to break through, but to no purpose. Lally was penalised for a, foul charge, and Wattie Davies placed a goal. Just before the finish Ince had his kick charged down by Thomas, and that player hada clear run in. No goal followed. Result : —Batley 2 goals and 2 tries (10 points), Widnes nil.

LEIGH v. ST. HELENS. At Leigh, before 4,000 spectators. St Helens had the best of the opening stages,and Harris was making a dash for the line when be was badly'iripped by Lee, one of the home forwards.Mr.McCut cheen the referee,promptly ordered the latter off the field after eight minutes' play. rho Leigh forwards heeled out near the centre, but Woonward was too slow in gathering the ball, and Hill rushed up, dribbled down the field, and crossed to Flanagan, who scored for St. Helens, J. Greenwood fail- ing at goal. Several attacks by Leigh were fruitless, but eventually, after good passing by Bennett and Isherwood, Neville scored a brilliant try near the corner, Clarkson failim at goal. As half-time the score was a try each, Leigh on resuming attacked vigorously. Bennett passed to Neville, who got his second try, Woodward failing at goal. St. Helens were. dangerous several time, but Clarkson was cool, end eventually after judicious play by Sam Johnson, Isherwood scored, no goal resulting. After more fine back play Isherwood got an opening, and out-running , the St. Helens backs obtained his,second try, Sam Johnson kicking a goal. Result—Leigh, 1 goal, 4 tries (14 points), St. Helens, 1 try (3 points).

div.p: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF nEFORMERS.
XVIII.---if it is possible to "tax the foreigner," why does Protec- tionist Germany izvy an Income Tax on working men, and why is she about to raise domestic taxes heavily.

Protectionists say: Why not tax the foreigner? If that were possible no Protectionist nation would need to levy taxes at home. As a matter of fact, to take Germany as an example, most of the German States levy an 'income tax which reaches right down the scale. THE PRUSSIAN INCOME TAX ILLS TO BE PAID ON INCOMES AS LOW AS 17s. 3D. A WEEK'. The German Empire is in great financial diffi- culiies, and now (September, 1908) her statesmen are proposing many new schemes of domestic taxation, in spite of the recent raising tif the tariff. Why do they not " tax the foreigner?" L. G. C. 11.

div.head: LEITERS TO TIRE EDITa
div.p: LEITERS TO TIRE EDITa
ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS. LABOR OMNIA. VINCIT.—Owing to pressure on our space we base been compelled to hold over your letter till next week.—ED. "Ex. The Challenge to a Debate.

div.head: copy.
div.p: copy.

Dear Sir,—ln reply to ycurs of the 12th, our Committee are still very anxious that a set Public Debate should take place in Warrington between a representative of the Tariff Reform League and a nominee of ours. We are willing that a member of the Progressive Labour League should meet any person you may care to bring forward, whether a member of your League or not, and we sincerely trust that the Tariff Reform League will accept this challenge. Yours faithfully, JNO. MORTON ) joint J. IIOWES, Jun. f Secretaries. The Hon. Secretaries, Warrington Tariff Reform League.

div.head: Li'. Ramsay Macdonald and the National Service League.
div.p: Li'. Ramsay Macdonald and the National Service League.

Sir,—l am going to trespass on your kindness again by asking you to insert these additional remarks on Mr. Macdonald's unseemly attack on Lord Roberts and his followers. Mr. Macdonald states "that they were not going to allow a military system to ride over them either with spurs or without. By this I suppose he means tkat they are not going to allow any party to thrust com- pulsory military training upon an unwilling people. -Evidently Mr. Macdonald is as ignorant of the ideas of the League as he is discourteous in his attack on one of the finest soldiers this country has ever produced. Lord Roberts and his League, being profoundly con- minced that compulsory military training is vital for the well-being of this country, have set themselves the task of persuading the nation that the training proposed is necessary, just and advantageous. Now we recognise perfectly well that unless the great majority of the electors can be persuaded of this it is not only 'hopeless but undesirable to try to legislate in this direction. We have, however, such confidence in the sound judgment _of the people in the long run that we feel it only requires a few years more educa- tion to make the people realise the very great advan- tages of the system proposed. We believe that the people of this country do not desire to see their land again in such a defenceless and consequently dangerous position as it was during the Boer War when 50,000 trained troops could have marched from one end of the country to the other. Yet if the regular army has to leave these shores again—and who will say that this may not happen in the years to come—we are little better off than during the South African War. We believe, moreover, that day by day the man in the street is coming to realise that compulsory military training is far juster than the present system of trading on the patriotism of a few. Take for example the case of two youths Henry end Harold. Henry is in the Territoriids, Harold is not. The country is invaded. Henry keing a Territorial goes to the front 'and is killed. Harold being a non-combatant remains at home. Where is the justice in this ? Where again is the justice in allowing your la-di-da fellow whose gospel in life is summed up in the simple formula "Why Worry" and 'whose chief preoccupation seems to be the crease run- ning down his trousers, to continuo to sneer at Saturday afternoon heroes? Why shouldn't he be com- pelled to do something for the safety of the country? Lastly, we are convinced that the four months' training proposed is coming to be looked upon as dtsirable if only for the physical advantages which would accrue from it—that it is indeed no exaggeration to chritten it the Giant Doctor which would tone up many thousands whose vitality is depressed by the smoke laden atmosphere of our towns.—l am yours etc., Warrington, GEORGE CROSFIELD. February 10th, 1009.

div.head: PALACE MID HIPPODROME,
div.p: PALACE MID HIPPODROME,

Those who like to see a bright and amusing show are admirably catered for at the Palace and Hippodrome this week. Anything more laughable than Mike Craig's comedy turn it would be difficult to imagine, lie is assisted by his clever little dog which seems to revel in the show, and tho pair provide a lively quarter of an hour. Ted Waite is a Lancashire comedian with a quaint style, and bis song about " pals," girls, wives and " kids " is ore of the bits of the evening. The Galli- more Trio of comedy artistes add to the merriment with a turn full of fun and variety. One of the most pleasing features of the programme is a series of impersonations of music ball stars by Ruth Molloy, xho is an expert at this-kind of mimicry. She brings down the house with her portrayals. The Fordyces are capital singers and dancers, but excel in the latter accomplishment—in fact, they are two of the smartest dancers ever seen here. Kinnard, the magician, casts his spell over the audience and qnite mystifies them by producing rabbits and pigeons from the most unexpected. places. Lillie Luraine, musical speciality artiste, is a taleuted per- former on a number of instruments, her solos on the cornet being brilliant. Feldman's beau-ideal troupe of juveniles give a novel and creditable entertainment in which mimicry, song and wince are pleasingly combined. The biograpb pictures depict the awful destruction wrought by the earthquake at 3lessina and also show some of our "handy men" engaged in the work of succouring the injured. As usual the orchestral selections are admirable and the whole entertainment reaches a high standard. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

There should be crowded houses next week when the chief attraction will be Fred Karno's colossal. produc- tion "The Football Match,"—the struggle for supremacy between the Midnight Wanderers and Middleton Pie. Cans. Harry Weldon will appear in his famous part of " Stiffy," the goalkeeper, and characters will also be taken by Will Poluski, jun., and other well-known artistes. Other items will be provided by :—Cestria, comedy juggler and acrobatic waiter; Hicks and Bunter, vocalists and ice skate dancers ; Harvey and Holt, comedy speciality artistes ; Decima Brooke, dainty comedienne and dancer ; Walker and May, coloured vocalists and dancers (Walker is said to be the only blind comedian •in the world) ; Elton and Edwin, the world's premier banioists ; Sisters Hampel, the comedy couple.

div.head: TERRITORIAL CHURCH PARADE.
div.p: TERRITORIAL CHURCH PARADE.

Following on the lines of the Lindon Territorials, whose recent recrUitina efforts have met with such marked success, the West Lancashire Division Terri- torial Force have decided to lu ld a Church Parade on Sunday February 28th, in which each unit under its jurisdiction will participate. The Warrington Territorial Battalion (4th Battalion. South Lancashire Regiment) otend Divine Ser- vide at St. Peter's Church at 10.30 a.m. on February 28th. It is earnestly hoped that all who contemplate joining the local battalion, which has rendered such excellent service in the post as Volunteers whether in South Africa or on the more peaceful slopes of Salis- bury Plain, will do so on the-earliest possible occasion so that Warrington may not be behindhand in furnish- ing a full strength Battalion on the occasion of the Royal Review and presentation of new colours by his Majesty the King in Knowsley Paik during July. It IS rather an appropriate coincidence that the church parade will take place on the anniversary of the relief of Ladysmith.

Baptist Church - In connection with the Bazaar to be held March 24th to 27th in Parr Hall, en behalf of the Extension scheme, an excellent entertainment arranged by the Misses Hankey was given on Thursday evening in the Crosfield Dining Hall by kind permission of the firm, cbtained through the good offices of Mr. W.Olatworthy The Cromfield Orchestra gave selections and the pro- gramme included action songs, dances, a. dialogue and a tatbleau "Britannia the Pride of the Ocean."
