div.head: GUILDS OF HELP.
div.p: GUILDS OF HELP.
The Conference at Bolton.

The second National Conference of Guilds of Help was held in the Town hall, Bolton, on Wednesday. The Mayor of Bolton presided at the opening pro- ceedings and offered to the delegates a very hearty welcome' not only as the Civic head, but as President of the Bolton build of Help.. He said that he, personally, was very much interested in the move- ment and whilst some might think that opening new channels of philanthropy might be overdone, yet Guilds of Help were not intended to, nor did they supplant existing charities. They assisted other agencies in their efforts and prevented overlapping. They were not to be looked upon as doling-out Societies, but, through jersonal service, to provide a friend for those in need of help and advice. There were many advantages to be derived from co-opera- tion, and it was highly satisfactory to find that there had been inaugurated upwards of fifty societies. The first paper "The Relation of Guilds of Help to Public Authorities," wea read by Mrs. Florence Moser, of Bradford. When she was asked to prqpiie a paper for this Conference, she expected, she said, that the report of the Royal Commission on Poor Law would hnvfs been issued, and that it would contain very s s aenruto recemmendation3 on tho co-ordination of Public and Voluntary Relief Societies. Various fore- casts of this report had been made, but there was no definite indication of the way in which public relief duties might be entrusted to voluntary workers.ln con- sidering future methods of co-operation with public relief administration, they must examine a little into the reasons that have probably led to the wholesale condemnation of our poor Law System, which was the result of the inquiry. She could not help thinking it was just, because the Poor Law had made so little use of the voluntary element in its work that it had proved so unsatisfactory. Guilds of Help were pre paring to give this service. In many cases where children were ill-nourished and mentally or physically defective, the meals or training at school might do much, but if conditions in the home were bad, sleep- ing rooms ill-ventilated and overcrowded, food unsuitable, bad habits neglected, how could the meals and four or five hours at school avail much unless conditions in the home, where the rest of the 21 hours were spent, could be improved. The seine thing applied to the care and feeding of infants and to those who have returned provisionally cured from Consumptive Sanatoria. Everyone knew that, in the latter case, if they returned to former unsuitable . employment, or gave up sleeping with open windows or other good habits learnt in the Sanatorium, they would soon relapse, and all would be undone and wasted. The Bradford Guardians had recognized the useful part the Guild of Help could take in this work, and had set an example in co-operation between public and voluntary relief societies by subsidising the Guilds administrative work. In cases discharged from Hospital, such as the maternity eases leaving the Workhouse hospital, when the young mother first faces the world again with the new life given to her cherge and adding to her burden, where a wise and guiding hand may htlp her to make a good start and save her from disaster, the friendly helper could be invaluable. It was necessary to secure an adequate number of workers. Helpers must have an earnest desire to learn to be efficient to recognise that love and generous instincts were not enough, and that if they wished to be able to help and to teach they must be ready to learn. Order must be brought into the present chaotic conditions of charitable work. This saving of wasted effort would do much to provide the necessary workers, who were beginning to recognise the futility of the old methods of the lady bountiful with her patronage, her blankets and doles. Mr. Alderman Fildes, of Manchester, read the next paper, "The Relation of Guilds of Help to Charities." He said that local circumstances - would always govern the development of a new institution. ' The whole subject turned inevitably on the question of whether or not it was advisable to give relief. Manchester was in most ways specially suitable for the development of a Guild on the" no relief" principle, by reason of its many relief-giving agencies. Guilds cncl not demand anything from other institutions. Charitable institutions were only too pleased to avail themselves of any assistance which would make their work more useful and efficient. The idea which they were trying to realise in Manchester was to allow the responsibility for giving any charity to be entirely in the hands of independent organisations each specially fitted to deal with certain kind of cases, and each pre- pared to co-operate with the other organisations in a definite policy embracing the activities of all. The helper acted as an investigator, he was a scout ahead of the main body who were fighting against poverty. He reported cases, watched them -while in receipt of relief, and reported any change of circumstance which might affect the policy of the institution, and more especially when the time of strain and trouble was over, he was able through the friendly relations established, to contioue the aftercare and see that steps were taken to prevent a similar breakdown in the future, and prevent the consequent lass of char- acter and independence.

Immediatelysafter lunch, Mr. Arthur Lowry, of the Local Government Board, road a paper on "The Unemployed and public provision for the assistance since 1834." He assumed that his hearers were familiar with the history, from the decay of the Feudal System until the year 1831, of the experi- ments and expedients adopted by the legislature and society to deal with the problem of the workless. He went into the five methods found prevalent of afford- ing relief to able-bodied men and which the Royal Commission of 1884 described in their report, viz. : (1) Relief without labour, (2) The Allowance System, (3) The Roundsman labour, (2)The Allowance System (4) Parish Employment, (5) The Labour-rate System. He traced the different Orders and Minutes and gave extracts from Acts of Parliament, reports of Commissions and Committees, and other official documents, but purposely kept out of sight his personal views and ?pinions._

- In a minute dated November 20, 1869, on the reref of the Poor in the Metropolis, the late Lord G-oschen, then President of the Poor Law Board, referred to the great success with which Poor Law Authorities and the administrators of charities worked together at the time of the cotton famine.

Immediately after the passing of the Unemployed Workmen Act a Royal Commission was appointed to enquire into the Poor Law and the relief of distress. Distress Committees and Boards of Guardians were, therefore, sub judiee, and nothing would induce him to incur a charge of contempt of court. (The Report was issued the same evening.) Time would show what the outcome would be of the recommendations of the Roya! Commission, and their considera- tion by statesmen, but whatever statutory bodies might in the future have to deal with the problem ry of distress, and whatever might be their constitution and• powers, it could hardly be doubted that a great work must remain for such an organisation as the Guild of Help. Destitution was a disease in the body politic. The sufferers might be classified according to the chronicity, periodicity or acuteness of the attack, and might be treated by this or that public authority, and satisfactory cures might not be infrequent. But where the disease had once been there was too often danger of a relapse, so that prevention was better than cure. This was a truth which had been generally seized and acted upon by the much maligned Boards of Guardians in the case of children of the destitute.

The field open to a body such as a Guild of Help was wide. They might leave the destitute altogether alone if they would, and yet find abundant work to be dono among the poor and friendless, By the well directed influence of individual upon indi.rzcivatthey could anticipate and check the beginnings of reliance upon rate or tax and secure the preservation of that personal independence which, far more than the franchise, was the hall mark of the complete citizen. At this stage of the proceedings aftersoon tea was served in the Mayor's dining-room—an interval of pleasing diversion when one could meet the many enthusiastic supporters of the movement and chat as to the various methods of organization and resource. Afterwards a paper, "The place of relief in the service of the poor, was read by Mr. W. Grisewood, of Liverpool. They might admit at once, he said, that the giving of material relief of anything which the recipient had not earned by his own exertions— was attended with great danger, was very apt to loosen his moral fibre, and, especially in weak natures, to induce him to lean upon other support than his own exertions ; this danger must be avoided. On the other hand, they must not forget that there was also great clanger in leaving a man struggling with adversity, without the help that was necessary even to enable him to continue the struggle. After manfully endeavouring" to maintain hiri own independenee,be might sink into a state of discourage. ment and despair, from which a friendly hand, and well-placed help, might have reamed him.

div.head: amm,
div.p: amm,

It was a commonplace in economics that the giving of material relief in supplementation of a man's earnings tended to bring about a-reduction of wages, not only in his own case, but in that of others in the same line, and there could be no doubt that this was a consequence whenever relief was given in such a way as to became a reliable sonrcs of ineomc, but it was quite open to question whether the ' condition of the wage earners would not be still more depressed by their remaining with quite inadequate means of maintenance, which might compel them to ' accept lower wages. He gave instances that had come before his own notice.

In Liverpool, where they claimed to have a nearer approach to Elberfield methods than existed in any other part of England, applications for assistance wire received through the Central Office. These were all investigated by their own official agents, in order that the minimum of information, requisite to the formation of a proper judgment as to the circumstances, personal abilities and fixture prospects of the family, might be secured. If a case urgently required temporary help, their official agents were authorised to give it in the form of orders for food and fuel. The whole of the case Papers, when complete, were forwarded to the Friendly Visitor of the section in which the arplioaut resided, who at no called, and used his judgment respecting the case, giving further temporary relief if necessary, and reporting the whole matter at the next meeting ti he comthittee of the district in which the section was situated, of which he was a mereber, which thereupon considered what was the best to be done, in order that by contemporary assistance, or other means, the applicant might be helped towards self-support in the immediate or near future. This system was found to give satisfacbry results. They must not, however, lose sight cf the fact that there was a large _section of those dependent who had become such by their own inherent weakness or faults of character, and from whom, judginc, by their past, they; could not expect, until happily a change was wrought in , their character, any effort to second plans for their beneat. It was still their duty, parhaps a mare obvious duty in these than in other cases, to do their best, in co-operation with religious and moral agencies to stimulate in them a desire for better things. but he was quite convinced that it would be a mistaken policy for them to undertake any material assistance. Interesting discussions followed the reading of each of the papers and much satisfaction to those interested in the work of Guilds of Help was derived therefrom. " How to deal with distress caused by intemperance and wastefulness (with special reference to the Children's Act) was down for the evening's meeting but the Writer and the Rev. W. 13racecamp, who listened to the other papers, were unable to remain. EDMUND OSBORNE.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND HUMES.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND HUMES.
Rugby Football.
By " Ovalist."

Will Warrington stagger the football world again ? There are distinct psssibilities about the engagement at Oldham, and the Warrington men, led on by a big bright bonus and the prospects of glory, may do something desperate to the Watersheddings contingent. They were the first team to heat Oldham this seaxon, and as they were superior to the extent of 27 points on that occasion they ought to be equal to gaining the verdict to-day. Of course, Oldham have something to wipe off the slate, and as they have not lost on their own ground for over two years they will doubtless feel quite suro of humbling Warrington. It is the contemplation af that proud record that I find so encouraging. It can't last for ever, and on present form Warrington ought to smash it. Play up Wire- pullers!

There is likely to be a considerable following from Warrington, for it is years since there was so much enthusiasm about a League visit to the hilly, milly town. And granted a continuance of the spring -like weather the contest between two such teams should he worth the-journey to witness. I would like to draw my readers' attention to the fact that Messrs. Dean and Dawson, Ltd., are running a special excur sion from Warrrington Central Station at 1.30 to Clegg-street, Oldham.

The Warrinegton team is fortunately at full strength and will be the same as last week, viz.: Tilley, full back ; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor, and Treharne, three- quarters ; Brooks and Jenkins, half backs ; Thomas, O'Neill, Dowell, Shugars, A. Boardman and Belton, forwards.
_ -- C-. W. Smith, the ex-New Zealander, has been appointed trainer of the Oldham team.
Oldham have selected their strongest side, viz., Wood; Tyson, Smith (G. W.), Llewellyn, Oldershaw ; Avery, Beynon ; Ferguson, Smith (A..), Longworth, Wright, Jardine and Wilkinson.

Those people who imagined that the second fixture with the Australians would be tame and uninteresting because it was a " friendly" were vastly mistaken. Both sides were determined to win, and one of the keenest and most exciting games seen at Wilderspool for along time was the result. A draw was a very fitting result on the day's play, and neither side could claim the monopoly of the honours. It was rather a surprise to find the Australians so good, for of late they have not been winning matches, whereas War- rington's recent progress has been one of triumph. Most people expected the locals to win in handsome fashion, but for once in a way they met their equals on their own turf. The Kangaroos put up a fine per- formance, especially in view of the fact that Warrington bad beaten them 10-3 earlier in the season. Personally, I thought that as a result of their tour the Australians were a much improved and stronger team.

There is one thing that each side could claim, and that is each was unforttinate in not winning. War- rington had a try by Dickenson disallowed by what seemed an error of judgment on the part of the referee. On the other hand lam quite certain that he made a mistake in the closing moments of the game which probably robbed the Australians of the match, The incident was a peculiar one. Frawley had equalised the scores —8 points all —by running over at the corner. He pretended to touch down, deceived Fish, and ran unopposed behind the posts, where a certain place-kick would have given his side the victory. The referee was clearly of the opinion that Frawley had touched down at the corner, and made him take the try at that point, notwithstanding protests from the visitors. I saw the whole movement pretty clearly, and am convinced that the scorer never pat the ball within six inches of the turf. He was never tackled and had an easy chance of working the bluff. Because it failed I think the Australians were unfortunate, and at any rate Warrington had a lucky escape. It was a lesson that even Fish learnt cheaply.

Much of the excitement of the game was due to the way the lead alternated from one side to the other. It was a novelty to Warrington to be behind at the interval, but less than ton minutes from time they seemed to hava the match wlti. Then came Frawley's try in the last minute and the points were halved. There was not as much open play as is usually seen at Warrington, but both sides watchA one Another very keenly and many promising movements were nipped in the bud. The Australian forwards scrum- maged rather more loosely than should have been allowed, but they played a fine game and frustrated many of Warrington's dangerous movements at the base of the scrum. The home side was best at three- quarter, but nowhere else could they claim much advantage, and even here one man practically neutral- ised their general superiority.

I refer to Messenger, the Australian skipper. No Rugby enthusiast needs to be told that he is a great player. Personally I question whether there MB ever a greater, or one who could influence the play of a team more. On Saturday he played a marvellous game and frustrated Warrington time and again. One or two individual feats by him fairly " brought down the house "—for instance, the pick up, when running at full speed, from the feet of the home forwards. But in addition he was responsible for every point the Australians got, scoring a goal and a try himself, and making the opening for Frawley_in single-handed fashion right at the close. As a football asset, there is no estimating his value. Rumour says that be will eventually wear the Warrington colours. I can only hope that ?tumour is not this time a lying jade. If there is any chance of securing him I am sure the members of the Club would agree to pawn the pavilion should any such sacrifice be needful,

div.head: er, Saturday, February 20, 1909.
div.p: er, Saturday, February 20, 1909.

Two of the features of the play on the Warrington side were the keenness and cleverness of Fish, who well earned his fine try, and the way Tilley was out- manouvered time and again by Messenger's wonderful punting. I don't blame the Warrington cuPtodian. He is a/grand full back, but he had practically two full backs to cope with in Messenger and Hedley. The former was an extra-everything and roamed all over the field. He seemed to magnetise the ball and paralyse Warrington. There was ample excuse for occasional slips by the home defence. Another word of praise should be accor led O'Neill, who again proved what a resourceful player he is in the loose. At times he is equal to an extra threequarter, and can make an opening with the best.

On many occasions they have been beaten by an odd point in club matches, and yet they are able to give the full strength of the Union a level .game. In the third test match at Birmingham on Monday they were beaten by one point —6-5 after having the best of the game, and being without illeasenger. Had the skipper been able to play there is no question as to which side would have won. Half an hour of his genius would have given the tourists a safe margin. Luck seems to have deserted the side, and they are to be sympathised with in not winning one of the three test games. The first ended 22-22, the second 5-15, and the third 5-6.

div.head: Hockey
div.p: Hockey

Tbe meeting between Latchford and Waterloo last week was producive of a fine game of hockey. The sides were very evenly matched. Tnerer was no scoring in the first half. Afterwards Parker obtained the lead for Latchford and Waterloo equalized. End to end play followed ajad in the last part of the match a couple of smart goals by Travis and Parker gave Latchford the victory by 3-1.

The second string defeated Manchester Y.M.C.A. at Alexandra Park by 7-0. The game was a good one despite the one-sided score. Minards was again top scorer with 4 goals and the others were obtained by Warburton (2) and Knight (1). The Y.M.C.A. defence broke down badly on several occasions.

To-day the return matches with Winnington Park are played. The first elevens are at Winnington. Latchford's team is ;—W. Unsworth, goal; C. Plinston, T. Dixon, backs ; F. Newell, J. B. Wilkinson, J. Albinson, halve 3 ; D. Travis, H. Parker, H. Scott, E. Banks, W. Spensley, forwards. Refereu, Mr. W. B. Cobb. Bus leaves Bridge Foot 1.30 p.m.

The second teams are at Latchford. The home players are :--H. Carter, goal ; J. Wilkinson, W. H. Pickles, backs; L. Keuworthy, A. Knight, F. Tole, halves ; H. Booth, A. Newton A. B. Starkey, W. H. Minards, C. Hackney, forwards. Referee, Mr. H. Warburton. Bully-off 3 p.m.

div.head: SECONDARY SCHOOL CONCERT.
div.p: SECONDARY SCHOOL CONCERT.

The fourth annuli, concert in connection with the Warrington Secondary Shoot, which was held in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening, was undoubtedly the most successful and enjoyable yet given by the pupils of this school. There was a large audience and a varied and high class programme was received with every manifestation of approval. The first part of the enter- tainment, which had been arranged by Mr. R.H.Albery, consisted of a performance of the cantata "The Picnic" (J. R. Thomas) by the school choir and orchestra. In every respect the interpretation of this bright and tune- ful music was most praiseworthy and special mention must be made of the solists, Violet Brown and Ernest Parsons, each of whom possesses a sweet voice and sang with taste and expression. Other pleasing features were duets by Mary Hackett and Lilian Norton, Arthur Greenough anct Benjamin Farrar, and trios by Mary Hackett, Benjamin Farrar and Dorothy McNeil, Ernest Parsons, Mary Hackett and Dorothy McNeil. After the cantata the audience had quite a feast of Gilbert and Sullivan, no fewer than four items from the operas of these great collaborators being given in succession. The duet and semi-chorus " Prithee, pretty maiden" from " Patience " was nicely sung, Mary Bamforth and Ernest Parsons taking the duet. Ernest Parsons sang the solo "The Magnet" from "Patience", in capital style, and an exceptionally charming and picturesque item was the fairy solo and cherus from lelanthe," the soloists being Hilda Binks and Kate Grocott. Vera Collin and Benjamin Farrar sang the ear-haunting duet "The Merryman and his maid "from "The Yeomen of the Gaard " with splendid effect, which was heightened by the semi-chorus and dance by a contingent of girls in pretty costumes. A clever variety entertainment of a humorous character by selected boys proved very popular. This closed the second part of the programme, for which Ansa B. Dawson, Miss E. Wilkinson, Mr. J. B. Baxter and Mr. A. E: Hoyle were responsible. The con Cert concluded with several scenes from "The Rivals" (R. B. Sheridan) which, for such youthful performers, were remarkably well presented. The characters well!! taken as follows: Mrs. Malaprop, Ethel Cooper: Lydia Languish, Ruby Witts ; Sir Anthony Absolute, Robert Ormsby; Captain Absolute, William H. Rigby ; Bob Acres,Thornas Amos; Sir Lucius O'Trigger,William Sbufflebotham. The play bad been arranged by Miss E. Frost and Miss E. M. Congdon. During an interval in the programme selections on the organ were given by Albert Dumbill. The concert throughout was a distinct credit to the school and hearty congratulations must be occorded to the Principal (Mr. E. S. A. Robson), the staff and the pupils upon the complete success of the enterprise.

div.head: Holy Trinity Congregational Tea.
div.p: Holy Trinity Congregational Tea.

The annual congregational tea and entertainment in connection with the above church was held in the schoolroom, Museum-street on Thursday evening. About 180 members of the congre:ation and friends sat down to tea. Afterwards a high-class entertain- ment was given including the following items : Pianoforte solos" Gavotte Imperial" Ballade (Chopin), by Mr. T. W. Pearce ; songs, "Angus Macdonald " and " Good-bye "by Miss Davenport; " The last Watch," by Mr. J. A. Westhott ; waltz song from" Merrie England" and "Orange Blossom." by Miss M. Houghton; "rho Trumpeter" and Joemas Wedding," by Mr. J. W. Bibby; humorous song, " Singers and Talkers " and " Singers and Songs" by Mr. G. H. Smith ; humorous readings by Mr. H. M. Ashton. All the artistes acquitted themselves most admirably and the entertainment was a complete success.—Daring an interval the Vicar (Rev. E. CE. Carleton) delivered an address thanking 'all the ladies who had kindly con- tributed trays, etc., also Mr. Hesketh (Sunday school secretary) and Miss Longdin for their indefatigable efforts in arranging the excellent programme. Miss Houghton, Miss Longdin and Mr. P. Salith acted as accompanists.

div.head: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING.
div.p: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING.
Further Criticisms.
• ARTICLE It. And sometimes we are devils with ourselves, When we will tempt the frailty of our powers, Presuming on their changeful potency. From " Troilus and Cressida."

After diligent search through writings o( naval and military authorities of this country, it is clear there is a wide divergence of opinion as to our liability to invasion. If experts so markedly disagree how is it possible for the people to judge? On the whole, expert opinion and let me add, commonsense, are not to be found on the side of the League. Ido not possess the requisite knowledge to discuss the technicalities involved in this question, but one thing I do know namely, it is financially impossible for this country, though it be the richest in the world, to maintain the Navy at a little more than a Two Power Standard—whatever this phrase may mean —and a conscriptionist army. Of course our friend will tell us that the cost of the latter will be comparatively email. Neither he or his friends can possibly commute the oost. On paper it may be quite easy to reckon, but in practice, as often happens, things work out quite differently. It is impossible to give a guarantee of cost in view of possible friction that might reasonably be expected to arise, were their proposals put into practice. Tke people of this country, more parti- cularly those on the Continent, are already over- burdened by the weight of costly and non-productive Naval and Military systems. National debts serve to remind us of the kind of legacies, which War and preparations for War leave behind for future genera- times to grapple with. Money is urgently required not to destroy, but to sustain life. Of course, this citizen army will only be utilised for purposes of home defence ! This is a prominent assertion of the League. But what guarantee can they possibly give that this will be rigidly adhered to ? Suppose another part of the Empire, say Canada; is attacked. Will this citizen army stay at home, or be compelled to go abroad to the seat of conflict ? Pushing this point to its logical conclusion, I cannot see how it can be otherwise than that this scheme would ultimately strengthen that aggressive Imperialism whose fruits we so bitterly know. In most of these controversies between experts one indispensible feature is usually overlooked and this is overwhelmingly important. I now refer to our own behaviour. In spite of the persistence of these txvo quarrelsome factions, if the people remain firm and resolute in their friendship, there need be no felt of invasion. The only fear to dread is the inoculation of the peoples by this "virus" of militarism. "To secure Peace we must prepare for War." This oft-repeated precept. which is the corner-stone upon which the National Service League wish to build up great military system, is both catchy and delusive. It is a moral truism, but applied to the relation of modern peoples, from our point of view, is a dangerous and pernicious statement. Were it not for the grave moral issues that are involved in this matter, one would feel disposed to treat it with considerable levity. It is customary to speak of Germany and ourselves having hitherto been at peace with each other. No battle has been fought and people talk glibly of this as 'Peace.' An outward calm but not an inner peace. Tranquillity of mind cannot exist, side by side, with constant dread. This condition is not " pgace," but "armed fear." Fear begets fear, distrugt excites distrust. Confidence and sympathy produce like qualities. Suspicion creates an atmosphere in which confidence can never thrive and without faith in the sincerity and equity of each other's motives, hope can never rise to fulfil its fruitful mission. Suspicion chills friendship, warps sympathy and disintegrates the forces working for union. It is a withering and blighting influence. I fail to see how neighbouring communities can possibly establish peaceful relationships with each other by strengthening the sinews of war. We should keep ourselves in a state of irritability which would be continually alive to occasions of offence. He that is prepared to be offended readily finds offence. A jealous sensibility sees insults and injuries where sober men see nothing. It would make conflict dangerously easy through unworthy ambitions in • circles of influence.' It rests upon the reactionary principle that ultimately, might is the final appeal in settling a quarrel. Its effect upon the youth of our oountry would be to perpetuate a false and pernicious ' nationalism ' which is incompatible with the teaching of international ethics. It is foolish and regrettable that men will still persist in viewing man- kind in so many clear-cut groups by lines of demarcation that are largely artificial and mechanical, and especially to conceive of these groups known as nations, being natural enemies, instead of friendly communities requiring each other's assistance. Those things which the League seeks to produce would simply foster this restrictive nationalism and conse- quently increase international antagonism, by forging the nation into a fighting entity. It is difficult to foresee how such a unity can be produced out of the heterogeneous mass of political opinion which is present in this country. It ignores the growth of Internationalism. Geographical limits, accidents of birth and colour, count for a great deal. I readily admit, and rightly so, but surely these dis- tinctions are not primarily essential in our estimation of men. If nationalism retard the growth of Interna- tionalism, it is false and perversive. The danger consists in converting an internal and pacific sentiment into an external and open hostility. iaationalities can exist, side by side, for mutual aid, without a direct antagonism of interests. The poor old woman in the story has a great lesson to teach niany people. It was said of her on seeing the sea for the first time that she was delighted and exclaimed "It was grand to see something of which there was enough for everybody." This Inter-Dependableness of peoples is writ large across the great heart of mankind. This was one of the greatest moving ideas of the early Free Traders. Militarism prevents the growth of this fraternity between nations by keeping them divided in armed camps. :We do not forget our home because we care for the city nor our own city because we care for the country, neither do we forget the true interests of our country when we desire to co-operate with other nations in forming a great world—commonwealth. I firmly believe that the National Service League in seeking to promote Militarism,will retard the growth of this elevated sentiment towards a sane and an exalted internationalism.

" Tis the sublime of man Our noontido majesty—to know ourselves Parts and proportions of one wondrous whole! This fraternises man—this constitutes Our charities and bearings. One great evil it would create, namely, the sub- ordination of the civil to the military authority, and 'caste' would inevitably be increased and strengthened. It would so shape the nation that the military officer would possess pre-eminent power in the land and this is not conducive to progress. Mr. Townroe wants us to believe that his friends wish to democratise the Army. If the Army is not democratic under a voluntary system, it is difficult to realize how under compulsion the' duke's son 'and the 'labourer's son' would be treated on the basis of equality. BY compelling men to serve, grave moral issues arise which call for solemn consideration. Says Major Bellendene in "Old Mortality," "lam no politician, and Ido not under- stand nice distinctions. My sword is the king's, and when be commands I draw it in his cause." Such conduct is morally reprehensible. If might were right it would be different, but then, might is not always right. Let us enquire into' nice ' distinctions. Ilas any man a moral right to slaughter his fellow whom be has never seen before, and with whom he has bad no quarrel. But our battonal honour Imd Integrity have been impugned and etc., etc. S 3 runs the tale. It would be helpful if a careful diagnosis were per- formed on this 'national honour 'and the results of this examination placed in simple form before the people. Sentiment is even useful to our friends. Life is life wheresoever it be sacrificed and has everywhere equal claims to our regard. They who are shocked at a single murder, hear with indifference aye, and cheer when thousands of their enemy are slain on the field of battle. What a moral phenomenon! What gross inconsistency ! It is because men do not think of this iniquity that custom makes them so complacent and callous. It is said of the soldier that little more is reqiiired of him than that he be brave and strong. If, Irma whatever motive he resigns the direction of his c >millet to that of another, surely he cannot retain that independence of mind and moral uprightness, -which should be so highly treasured. And the implicit obedience to superiors implies the relinqnishment of our reasoning powers. But can a man so abandon his moral responsibility ? Either he is responsible for his actions or he is not, and the question is a most serious one. Personally, I cannot see how a roan can so readily cancel his moral obligations. This is well and characteristically expressed in the Biglow papers :

Ef you take a sword an' dror it, An' go stick a feller thro', Guv'ment aint to answer fer it, God'll send the bill to you. Writ's the use o' meotin' goia' Every Sibbath wet or dry, Ef it's right to go a-mowin' Feller men like oats and rye. John Aforley finely expresses the alma idea : —" What better service can a man do than to furnish the world with an example oft faithful dealing with his own conscience and with his fellows ? This, at least, is the one talent that is placed in the hands of the meanest of us all." It is pre-eminently an individual matter and not until each individual has solemnly considered his moral responsibilities will war be abolished. The attempt to prostitute our universities and schools to the service of militarism is a grievous wrong to the rising genera- tion, for it places a fatal stumbling block in the way of progress and civilisation. It his its source in absolutely false conceptions of the relation of man to man and nation to nation. Well might we ask " Is there not a better way ? " H. GRAY. Warrington. _ _ _
To be concluded.

div.p: MORE MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.
vigorous Speech by Mr. Dodds.

The Free Trade League's local campaign in support of our present fiscal policy was continued on Thursday evening when a meeting was held in the Thewlis-street schools. Mr. John Upson presided over a good attend- ance and WAS supported by Mr. John Whitworth (Bowdon), Mr. J. L. Leech (Manchester), Captain G. R. Crosfield, Councillor Hawthorn, Mr. S. Wright and Mr. J. Elwell; jun. Excellent speeches were delivered and well received and it is a sGurce of great regret to us that we have been unable to find room for a full report.

div.head: Meeting at Silver-street.
div.p: Meeting at Silver-street.

Last evening a meeting was held in thes Silver-street Schools, Mr. James Dodds presiding. The principal speaker was Mr. Edward Wakefield (formerly Colonial Secretary of New Zealand) who delivered a striking address on the advantages of the Free Trade system. There were also present on the platform : Councillor Skelland, Mr. E. Wynne-Jones, Mr. J. Elwell, jun., and Mr. Felix Maginn. MR. DODDS' DEFENCE OF FREE TRADE.

The Chairman said : - Last night, in the House of Commons, the leaders of the Unionist party fully and finally nailed the flag of Protection to their party mast. They may call them- selves Fair Traders or Tariff Reformers,. or whatever they consider most likely to•gull their victims, but their intention is that we shall revert ,to a flssal system abandoned over 60 years ago as being ruinous alike to trade, and to the well-being of this country. lam not here as a party politician, but I am here to maintail, so far as the issue raised in the official Tory Amendment to the address is concerned, I am here to maintain the principle of free imports, under which the wealth 'and the well-being of this nation has been doubled and trebled during that period. Although the great body of the Unionist party are now pledged to Protection under its latest name, the most thoughtful of its leaders, with the possible exception of Mr. Balfour—about whom no-one is even yet sure, are standing firmly by the principle and policy of Free Trade. Such men as Lord Hugh Cecil and Lord Robert Cecil—like their great father Lord Salisbury—Sir John Gorst, and many others realise that Tariff Reform meani Protection, and that Protection means a reversion to the starvation and the miseries of the "hungry forties." Tariff Reformers say that, if what they propose is Protection, it is very, very little Protection; but I appeal to the whole history of Protection over the whole face of the earth, when I say that protective tariffs once introduced, always tend to rise, and can never be beaten down except by great and prolonged effort on the part of the people. I repeat that

div.head: TAXES ON FOOD.
div.p: TAXES ON FOOD.

have always historically gone on rising until they cculd be borne no longer. And that will certainly follow here if you are so unwise as to back Protection under the name of Tariff Reform, and with terrible results. I wonder whether auyone here has any idea of the condi- tions under Protection in this country sixty or seventy years ago. Here is what Mr. Chamberlain said in 1885—I believe in Warrington "At that time the whole of the labourers in th e
agricultural districts were on the verge of starvation.

The poor rates in some districts were 20s. in• the Z. The larger towns were described, by eye-witnesses as having the appearance of beleaguered cities. So terribl3 was the misery that people walked the streets like gaunt shadows, and not like human beings. There were bread riots in every town, there was rick burning in every countryside; we were on the verge of revolution when the Corn Laws were abolished." That is what will inevitably follow a return to Protection. I give many supporters of Tariff Reform credit for not desiring this, but, as surely as the night follows the day, so surely would the evils of Protection develop, with all their consequent corruption and misery. Only a day or two ago, one of the most level- headed Unionists in the country, Lord Avebury, wrote :

"It is clear that duties on imports must raise prices. In fact, that was the reason Mr. Chamber- lain gave for not suggesting duties on bacon and maize, because, as he said, they were the food of the poor. But, if duties would raise the price of bacon and maize, it is obvious that they would also raise that of bread. Indeed, if they did not, how would they benefit the growers of wheat, either in the colonies or at home? But, if we are to have a wide tariff and a general rise of prices, life must necessarily become more expensive. The labourer, the artizan, the doctor, the lawyer, the clerk, the clergyman, in fact 95 per cent of our people, will find that they have to pay more for food, for clothes, for house rent, &c., and they will not, I believe, be so foolish as to incur the certainty of higher prices on - the chance of higher wages. The policy of the fiscal reformers is to revert to the wretchedness of the hungry forties,' and I cannot think that the county will support them in this retograde course. "As a firm Unionist, therefore, I deplore the recent action of Conservative caucuses, and cannot believe that the country will endorse a policy which may enrich a few, but only at the expense of the groat majority, and especially of the poor." In this connection, could anything have been more apposite and touching than the pathetic appeal made to his party in the House of Commons only last night by Lord Robert Cecil,—when he begged his leaders to stop the repetition on Tory platforms of

div.head: LYING STATMENT
div.p: THE LYING STATMENT

that Tariff Reform meant "work for all." Referring to this disgraceful practice, he said : "This kind of thing is not only disastrous from the party point of view, it will not only lead to disaster when you come into office, but it is really not a proper, a dignified, and a high-principled way in which to treat the starving multitude of this country. I earnestly ask you if, in regard to this particular branch of the subject, it is really too late to call a halt ?"

Lord Robert Cecil no doubt seas, as every thinking man knows, that Protection has in the past and would be more likely in the future, to intensify the evils of unemployment. It is now universally admitted that Protection would make things dearer. If things are rendered dear, then money would not go as far in buying things, and conse- quently there would be fewer things bought. If fewer things were bought, naturally there would be fewer things made • and if there were fewer things made, there would be less employment for those employed in making such things; and so it comes that unemploy- ment is greater in protected countries than in our own, though occasionally it is serious enough here. That Free Trade is a cause of unemployment, or that it intensifies unemployment is absolutely untrue. Take the building trade : it has been bad all through the boom in general trade, as I happen to know; you know that foreign competition, or Protection, or Free Trade, does not touch that industry, and yet, during the past 3 1 or 4 years, every morning almost, .I have been stopped by builders' labourers out of employment, begging for 1 the price of a breakfast. No,

9'llo. MAIN CAUSES ON UNEMPLOYMENT are not fiscal. If I were asked to suggest a remedy, I should be disposed to '.say : make the land available, force it into the market, double your building trade, and you would add a million hands to it, and thereby start machinery that would draw in and give work to all forms of labour. I would also seek to induce the people to red ace the National Drink Bill of £160,000,000. Only on Wednesday in the House of Commons, John Burns told the members that a Tory bank manager in a North of England town had written him that on Fridays he paid out from fifty thousand to sixty thousand a week for wages, and that,'of that money, from twelve thousand to sixteen thousand pounds came back to the bank from the publicans of the town on the Mondays. If the sum spent unnecessarily in drink— several shillings per week per family—was spent in better and more food, better and more clothing, batter and more furniture,and better housing, and in insurance against unemployment, there would be such an impetus given to trade and employment as would sot back the urgency of the unemployment question for a generation at any rate. But it would not probably make an end to the trouble of unemployment; for, wherever there is competitive industry—and there the Socialists are ritgfit—thers would be a tendency to some unemploy- ment.

These fiscal quacks, these Tani If Reforreers,profess to believe in" broadening the basis of taxation"; that is taking money out of your pockets and trying to make you believe it is out of the foreigners pocket,

All goods sold by us are manufactured in factories under our own control and supervision, from exclusive designs. We can thus guarantee to our Customers a well made article of useful as well as artistic design and substantial manufacture.
1/ PRICES T THE POCKET.

By controlling our manufactories we place the goods on the Market bearing one profit only—the goods going direct from us, the manufacturers, to our customer, the consumer—bearing only the one profit and not two or three as charged elsewhere.
To-day, mainly as a result of the giving of Old Ag! Pensions, we am o anticipating a budget deficiency 0' £15,000,000. Germany,

THE IDEAL STAMP: OF THE TARIFF REFORMERS has a deficit of £25,000,000; and in 10 years their deb, has gone up by £100,000,000, although they have had tu wars; so that, with their scientific tariff to make tls foreigner pay, they are faced with a £25,000,000 deficit Are the Germans going to raise this by bigger dutied against the foreigner, and if not, why not if, as thl tariff reformers here say, the foreigners pay? No the Germans are going to put higher duties on beer, all 4 spirits, and tobacco, and on death duties, and a duty 01 electric light. Does-not this prove that the Germsee know that it is the home consumer and 13° the foreigner who pays a country's taxee and so, the issue after all is whether, the interests 6? the landowners and of manufacturerl In this country, we are to raise all the cost of 01 people's food and of the consumer's raw and othe, materials, in other words,to raise rents and to multipi; Industrial millionaires. But, leaving this, surely chest ness in itself is an advantage. As Lord Hugh Cecil be well said :—" If a sovereign will purchase 3 article' under Free Trade, as against 2 articles under Protectiol It means more labour .” and it does not mean sweatisil Sweating is more likely to be induced when 110 materials are dear. In short, from all experience, a against Protection, free imports hair's meant cheaPel materials for the actual consumers or users, with bette wages and greater comfort for the toilers. I have detained you too long,or I should have liked tc show that dumping is an advantage to t 11( country dumped upon, and that preference to the Colonies, so far as practical proposals have been mole would not, indeed could not, work. One word on tbo latter point. It has been proposed to get our foreigt corn supply mainly from Canada. The ports 9 Canada are closed for four months of every year, sc that, if we were at war with America, most of our foo( would be at the mercy of one enemy. The Tail Reformers say they are practical; they propose to hell Canadian farmers who don't need help. If tanadiel farmers with virgin soil need assistance, what about till highly rented farmer here? What must his need be In a word, this proposed preference arrangement is corrupt one put forward in response to the demands o Canadian manufacturers, who having burdened 01( Canadian farmer more than he can bear, seek to sav4 him by laying additional burdens on the licks of th' workers of England. Protection, by whatever name you call it, is ever till child, aye and the PIRENT OF CORRUPTION. If our people should over be so misguided as to revel', to it, it will no doubt enrich the landowners and mso manufacturers, but this will be out of the starvatiof and the tears and the blood of the poor of Mere' England. But I have no fear. Yo.o will stand by frel, trade, and by all it means, the brotherhood of man, an‘ the federation of the world, aye and the Fatherhool of God! for its underlying principles are identici, with those which constitute the glorious attributes 0' His Eternal reign. (Applause.) A resolution affirming unshaken belief in Free Trade was adopted on the proposition of Mr. E. WVINJ JONES, seconded by Mr. WAKEFIELD.

Numerous presents were received, includini a beautiful clock from the Co-operative Glee Societi of which the bridegroom is tlia conductor.

With regard to the School Management Sub-com- mittee's estimates, in higher education there was an increase in secondary school teachers' salaries of from £1,690 to £1,835, due partly to the operation of the scale and also to the fact that a portion of the cost or cookery which was now taught at the school, was included. There was an increase, due to V•aii appoint- ment of two part-time teachers, in the School of Art salaries of £435 to £4BO. Technical School teachers' salaries decreased from £l,lOB to £976, and Branch Techical School salaries increased from £B5O to £996. There bad been a re-adjustment of the work. The expenditure on examinations increased from £llO to £l5O. There was no change in the amount for scholar- ships—£2oo. It could not seriously be contended that the responsibilities of the town could be met by such a small sum, especially when one realized how the item was made up and how the money was disbursed. The financial position ot the Grammar School had materially improved, and it was doubtful if any sum would be required from the local authority, but they were assured_ that if any sum were needed it would not be more than £2OO. Last year £4OO was required. Of the estimated receipts there was an increase of £l5O in customs and excise grant (Z 900. The Secondary School grant also increased by 4150 (Z 950 duo to the change in the Government method of paying grants. There was a substantial increase in the Branch Technical Schools grant—from £5BO to £9OO. That was welcome, because it indicated an increased attendance of students and improved organization as well. There was a decrease of £7O for pupil teachess (£330) due to the fact that the number had been reduced. ELEMENTARY EDUCATION.
